I quite agree with your ruling. I know I shall have ample opportunity to bring this matter up again. I want to thank the minister for his reference to the Royal Military College at Kingston.

I wish to make a few general remarks at this stage before we get into the details of the particular items in the estimates of the Department of National Defence. This morning the minister reminded the committee that last year there was a vote of $486 million for the department which he now heads, of which some $383 million was spent. Last year that estimate represented approximately one-quarter of the Canadian budget for all purposes. The amount spent was some $100 million less than the estimate, due to a speeded-up demobilization, for which some credit is due to the government with all the difficulties they had in that connection. This year I notice that about one-eighth of the entire budget is devoted to this department, roughly $240 million. As near as I can gather that is to be spent almost entirely on Canadian peace-time military expenses.
In his opening remarks the minister referred to certain general considerations of the organization of the peace-time forces. At the moment I am not concerned with the details. They can well be left to the staffs concerned, with whatever criticisms we may have here and there. I just wish to refer to the remarks of the minister in connection with the organization policy which he said it was the intention of the government to establish. He said the primary purpose was to defend Canada; the second purpose was to maintain law and order in Canada, and the third-and I am not too sure that I got him correctly in this, because I am a little concerned about it in part-was cooperation with friendly nations or to meet the demand of the united nations.
In . my view and in that of the party to which I belong, the C.C.F., the armed forces of Canada are not needed to maintain law and order in this country. As a matter of fact if hon. members go over the estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the past number of years they will see that there has been an enormous expansion in that field.

Supply-National Defence
There are other civilian police groups which have to attend to the enforcement of the laws of this country and of the provinces and of the municipalities. It seems to me that law enforcement in Canada should not be the primary role of the Canadian army. We are not a lawless nation. To put ahead of the objective, as I see it, of the Canadian armed forces-that of playing its part in the peace of the world in cooperation with the united nations organization-the maintenance of law and order among our civilians at home as an ideal for the organization, seems to me to indicate improper emphasis.
To refer to the first point that the minister raised in this connection, that the chief consideration of this large expenditure was the defence of Canada, I would point out that if the implementation of the present policy in the defence of Canada is, as it is now, in this interim force, using procedures which to me look very much like those of the old professional service days, then there are some terrific gaps still left to be taken care of. If we take the minister at his word and consider only the defence of Canada, the defence of the shores of this country, the methods he has outlined today are utterly inadequate.
If the minister thinks his department is laying the groundwork for the defence of Canada against attack by an outside aggressor, and that it is doing so by means of what he outlined this morning, I would ask him this question. Does he not believe that if this country is diue for an attack at any time we would have a general civilian participation in its defence? And that includes men, women and children. If that is so, has the minister indicated to the house, anywhere in his statement this morning, to what extent he is preparing the civilian population of the country for the defence of our home land?
Anyone who has the most elementary knowledge of military attack and defence knows that the brunt of defence is nowadays borne by civilians and not by trained troops, that is, by uniformed troops. If we are thinking in terms of air attack we must have our firefighting defences and our first aid equipment. We are undoubtedly going to have antiaircraft gunners and they will be drawn largely from the civilian ranks. The minister has made no reference at all to that form of training, and there is no evidence in his statement that he is making a realistic approach to defence against invasion from any source.
We have our troops employed after a fashion. W'e again have the procedure we had during the war, mentioned by the minister a few moments ago in answer to a question
by the hon. member for Yale, in which we are moving troops back and forth from one end of the country to the other over the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. To give added travel revenues to the railway companies because of a change in the decision of some officer on the national defence staff is not my idea of training troops for the defence of this country. What other means have we in this country, or has the minister indicated he intends to use in this country, for the rapid deployment of the forces that are being trained or that are about to be trained?
If the minister is really sincere in talking defence, he should tell us about some auxiliary transportation facilities other than the railways of the country. Not one word is mentioned in his report about highways, for example. I take that back in part, because I believe there is an item of some 810 million for the northwest staging route. We cannot possibly defend Canada by maintaining no other than that highway built during the last war by the United States. The government of this country, if it is going to follow realistically the policy which it has itself expressed!, must envisage a highway system in Canada such as we are not likely to see for many decades if the government of the day does not do any more about highways than it has done in the past.
We cannot move troops and equipment by these two ribbons that run across this country, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National railway. Where are our highways? Where are our feeder highways? If we are going to move troops and move them rapidly, if we are going to move ordnance supplies and other equipment, we cannot rely on railways or airborne transportation. The minister might have mentioned the Hudson Bay route. We have troops training in the north, but there is no indication that the military staff is realistic in its professed intention to defend Canada by using some of the avenues that nature has provided.
I maintain that the minister's department is still making an easy living for a military caste in so far as present defence plans in Canada are concerned, and, further than that, that it is going back to the old laissez-faire ideal which I had hoped was outmoded for war purposes, in which monopoly munitions makers or equipment purveyors are being cut in on the melon if and when a war should take place.
It seems to me that the minister is trying to build up a modern fighting machine. I will give him credit for good intentions, but he is using horse and buggy tactics that are
Supply-National Defence

definitely in disrepute. It seems to me that if we are sincere in defence procedure in this country there is a major field for the Department of National Defence, and that is in the utmost utilization of the research facilities of this country and the extension of these research facilities far beyond what is envisaged in the amount of money authorized for military research purposes.
I want for a moment to refer to what I think are still a number of hangovers from the demobilization period. The minister referred to the fact that some three-quarters of the military stocks, buildings and so on, had been disposed of. Surplus stores and establishments, to the extent of some two-thirds or three-quarters, had been disposed of through War Assets Corporation. Have we not a ridiculous picture here again? On the one hand the minister and his department are declaring stores and equipment surplus to War Assets Corporation, which will be sold or given away to the trade, and we immediately ask for some $200 million odd. Of course, I realize that some of this is for salaries, but there are large commitments again for additional equipment and I would like the minister to assure the committee that the stores that have been disposed of and the establishments that the Department of National Defence has declared surplus, particularly buildings, are such that in no sense are they duplicated by new contracts or new purchases by his department. We certainly do not want that continuous building and handing over and building that seems to go on so planlessly for the defence needs of the country.
It is well planned.

It is well planned, but for whom? Not for the Canadian people but for a few individuals who will make easy money out of the suckers, the Canadian government and the Canadian people. This group, the C.C.F., emphasizes the fact that interested groups can again hang like leeches to the governmen'ts skirts, and can again make a profit from the weapons of destruction in whatever form they may be, and that this policy is one of the contributing factors to war fever.	.
I was pleased that the minister this morning made a rather laughing reference to the so-called flying discs which for some days now have disturbed many of the good citizens of this country, because the hysteria as a result of which we can get into a war panic is so easily aroused. We must prevent such rumour spreading; we must make it unprofitable for anyone, whether it be the military caste in the seats of the Department of National

Defence or whether it be in the commercial organizations which profit when there is a war on. We want to still their voices, their gossip and their propaganda so that we can have a chance for this world to establish the peace in which every hon. member in this house is sincerely interested.
I was pleased to hear the minister state that his department is now willing to assume responsibility for living quarters for the married members of the interim and permanent force. After all, with our housing situation in this country as acute as it is, the department is best fitted to make accommodation available for those whom it employs in the forces of the country. I think that is a matter with regard to which either the minister's department owes this committee an explanation, or perhaps he can tell us that he has made the utmost use of the buildings which were in possession of the Department of National Defence for conversion into suites and quarters for the members of the forces. I want to compliment the minister for his humanity in taking the role of a benevolent employer and assuming the responsibility for providing the quarters in which the married members of the armed farces live.
Before the dependents' allowance board is closed off with respect to the last war, there are still quite a number of cases which the minister should investigate with respect to improper cutting off of the dependents' allowance paid. As hon. members will note from the wording of the regulations of the dependents' allowances board, it is not the-right of a dependent of a soldier, airman or naval rating to receive the allowance permitted by the regulations. That is, it depends on the whim, if you like, or the good wishes of the dependents' allowance board. To my mind that is a vicious principle. If in the future allowances are to be paid to members of families of serving personnel, those allowances should be theirs as of right once they are established as members of such families.
The minister referred to the fact that going wages were being paid to civilian employees of his department. To my knowledge, and by admission of the minister's own department, employees of the Department of National Defence in the city of Regina-at the Regina ordnance depot, to be specific-have not only not been receiving the going wage but in some cases have been receiving less than the minimum wage of $18.50 a week provided by the laws of Saskatchewan. I know the government of Canada is not bound by the labour law's of any of the provinces; that is, it is sovereign in that respect. But if we can

Supply-National Defence
throw away thousands and millions of dollars on pensions for the brass hats of the service- and I do not say that in the sense in which the hon. member for Temiscouata sometimes uses the term-and the higher officials of the professional services can receive pensions as high as $8,900 a year, surely the man whose sole income is the wages he earns, working for the Department of National Defence, is worth more than $18.50 a week.
In closing I would once more remind the minister that, if he is sincere in his suggestion that his department is intent on the defence of Canada, he should organize Canada so that it is a defensive unit. But, above all, while he is doing that-(because we have not yet made the united nations function as those of us who are its well-wishers hope it will function-I hope he will exert every effort of the Canadian government and the Canadian people to the end that the military set-up of the united nations be implemented at the earliest opportunity. Once again I should like to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the excellent contribution he made last winter when, on behalf of Canada, he spoke first before the united nations asking that the enforcement of the peace of the world be assured by a rapid and early setting up of defensive forces on a global basis, not on a bloc basis.

I rise at this time not to discuss defence in general but to get down to a little matter of detail, one which concerns part of our national defence which my small community might have to do with. The minister will know what I am talking about the very moment I mention that the community of Vulcan, Alberta, requires a drill hall.
That is right.

We have been working
on this matter for at least a couple of years. I have had several interviews with officials respecting the matter, and some with a previous minister of national defence. As I understood the situation we thought a drill hall was already in sight. Then about a month ago I was informed that perhaps a change would have to be made because there was no appropriation for that small project in this year's estimates. I interviewed the Minister of National Defence, who was very kind and courteous, and promised to look into the matter. I do not know whether he has a report as yet, but by this time perhaps he has and will be able to say something about it.
The amount included in last year's estimates for this undertaking was approximately $32,000. It was my understanding that a drill hall had been secured somewhere in the northern section of the province and that tenders were being called for its removal to Vulcan. Following that I understood something went awry but that a suitable building had been secured in the southern part of Alberta, which would have to be moved only about sixty miles. The people felt quite happy about that; then, much to our disappointment, this further information came to us. I do not quite understand why that item is left out of this year's estimates. Indeed, I do not know whether it is left out. As a matter of fact I doubt whether it would be technically correct to say it is left out of these estimates, because I expect that quite apart from parliament voting this sum, if this project has been left out at all the department has left it out of its own particular administrative orbit, in that it has not included the project as one of those to be undertaken.
As far as this parliament is concerned I do not know that we are particularly informed as to every project that might be involved in an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars. This appropriation amounts to $226,709,331 or nearly $227,000,000. The details appear o:i page 275, where I see an item of $14,348,558 or nearly $14,500,000 for the acquisition, construction, purchase, maintenance, repairs, rentals and operating expenses of properties. That is a considerable sum of money. I am not objecting to it at all, but I would point out that it is for new equipment and repairs, which means it is at least in addition to what the defence department already have by way of buildings as a result of the recent war. I believe this amount of over $14,000,000 is sufficiently elastic for the minister to include the Vulcan drill hall in the list of projects for this year.
Now may I say that my small community of Vulcan feels quite justified in asking for a drill hall for the reserve forces that train periodically in that district. They feel justified for more reasons than one. The community has a very proud war record. I know that is the case with all communities, but we feel that we can put the record of our community up against that of almost any other in Canada. It is only a small community. In the purchase of war bonds I believe we rank among the highest in Canada on a per capita basis; and the same applies even to such small matters as salvage campaigns. My own children came home wearing upon their arms stripes they had earned in a campaign to collect
Supply-National Defence

salvage. That is a small thing, of course. The Red Cross in our community has a wonderful record. Perhaps the thing of which we are prouder than anything else is that our war memorial, in the form of a cenotaph, has inscribed upon it the names of thirty-three young men, the very cream of the community, who gave their lives somewhere in the world during the last war. When I say this I am not boasting in any way, I say it in all humility. I know other communities have similar records, but I am stating these facts because to some extent we are dealing with public feeling. In spite of this record, to my knowledge the community of Vulcan has never asked the federal government for one nickel. That community has been on the contributing end of the nation's business. They are not sounding a grievance at all; they are proud of their efforts. Anything the town has it has obtained through its own efforts. We do not even have a publicly-owned post office, though very many communities of that size have such a building.
I say these things because I know if this town does not get this drill hall this year the people will feel extremely disappointed, and as far as I am concerned personally I will feel that the community has been slighted. I do not want to leave the impression that we are coming along asking for a favour. We are not. The community is asking that it might assist in our national defence programme, and that it be permitted to give that assistance under the most adequate conditions. That request, I think, is only reasonable. Furthermore I might say it is recognized by the departmental officials that such a project is needed. I wish to read a paragraph from a letter written by Colonel Snow, the officer in command of the western command. It is a letter that was recently received by a service club explaining why the $32,000 was not included in this year's estimates. In concluding his letter Colonel Snow says:
I am very sorry indeed that this matter has taken the course it has and I agree with you that Vulcan must have military accommodation very soon if our reserve force in that area is to continue to function.
If the lack of a drill hall means that the reserve force in Vulcan is not going to function, surely that is a serious matter. Colonel Snow is a highly respected official of the department and I think what he says should be enough for the minister now to say:	We
will do all we can for you.
I understand that the policy of the government in respect to these drill halls is to expect that they might be used for community recreational purposes as well, and I

agree with that policy, I think it is an admirable one, and since it is the policy of the government I suggest that our community has many small organizations without a place to carry on their activities. We have the boy scouts, the girl guides; we have cadets in that community; we have physical training classes and quite a few other movements of the kind. If it should rain, and I am sorry to say that we do not get much rain in that part of the country, but if it rains on the night on which one of these organizations is to meet, they have to postpone their meeting and stay home; nothing can be done. In the winter time their activities are almost non-existent. If a drill hall were constructed at Vulcan, the defence department would be doing a great deal for the community as well as in promotion of their own defence programme.
I have two suggestions to make. I suggest and urge as strongly as I can that if the minister cannot adjust his programme to include this project in this vote, he bring down a supplementary estimate to cover it. I do not want the minister to take advantage of my next suggestion, which is one that has been made by one or two of the organizations in that community; but if it is impossible for him to bring down an estimate for the construction of this drill hall, there is a recreation 'hall in the Vulcan air training school, which is situated about six miles out of the town. It would not be as satisfactory as a new drill hall, but perhaps it would be the next best thing; it would serve temporarily at least. It would have to be moved a distance of six miles, and I am suggesting that if it is impossible to go ahead with the plan for a drill hall as originally proposed, this recreation hall be moved and used for the purposes I have mentioned. I suggest that as the next best step. I understand that the building I have in mind has already been declared surplus. I must qualify that statement by saying that I did not. get the information from official sources, but I understand that is correct, and if it is, the building belongs to the national defence department.
In conclusion, I know that the minister has called for a report on this matter and perhaps there has not been time enough yet to get the report from the western command at Edmonton or Calgary, whichever it is. If the minister has not yet received that report,
I feel I know what his answer is going to be, that he will do his best to carry out my suggestion. I wonder if he can say to me now that something will be done about this matter this year. I want to thank the minister's parliamentary assistant for the time

he is spending on what might appear to be a very small thing when we are talking in terms of hundreds of millions of dollars. But it is not a small thing so far as that community is concerned. Mr. Chairman, I think I should reply to the hon. member for Macleod at once, because some other hon. members may have drill hall problems on their doorsteps and perhaps a brief statement as to the position might be useful.
I think nobody appreciates more than the department and the officers of the services the very strong desire which has been repeatedly expressed by reserve units and members of parliament and other community leaders for the provision of suitable armoury accommodation where that is not now available. I can assure all concerned that plans are being prepared to enable the department to proceed with a construction programme just as soon as the government feels that the time is ripe. My predecessor had hoped to begin last year with the construction of four or five different types of armouries in different localities so that we oould get on with the job and show our serious intent and also gain some experience. However, the shortage of housing accommodation was so great throughout the country that the feeling was expressed by the government, and I am sure was shared by members of parliament as well as by the people generally, that during these immediate post-war years we should deal with houses first. That is the policy of the government and of the department. As I have already pointed out, our target this year is to try to convert or construct over 1,000 new dwelling units for married personnel, thereby relieving the general pressure on housing accommodation throughout the country. On that account it has not been possible to calculate on making any new construction of armouries this year. I am sure that the hon. member for Macleod realizes that though his need is great and that of the reserve unit at Vulcan is great, there are units and places in Canada where the need is even greater. I know in the case of my old drill hall on Craig street, where they had only two major units before the war they now have four regiments of artillery and the Regiment de Maisonneuve. I can think of the drill hall at Quebec where instead of having two major units they now have four.
Can the minister think of the drill hall at Swift Current?

Yes, and1 also at
Edmundston, Saskatoon, and a few other places where the need is great. What we are doing is to try to convert existing buildings which were built by one or other of the armed forces during the war to be used on a temporary basis. This has been done successfully at Winnipeg and other localities.

That is the very thing I am asking for.
Mr. CLAXTO'N: I can assure the hon. member for Macleod that the matter he raised is receiving the most active consideration. We have not yet reached the point where we can carry out the alternative he mentioned. Wherever it is possible we will do that, and when later on circumstances permit I hope we shall be able to proceed with a long term programme of construction.

Mr. Chairman, I was glad to hear the minister say what he had to say to the hon. member for Macleod. The question of training quarters for our reserve units is one of great importance, and it should be receiving close attention even though there is a housing shortage in Canada. I hope the hon. member will get a drill hall, either on a temporary or permanent basis, as soon as possible.
I should like to try to wrench the hon. ministers mind away from the consideration of a drill hall at Vulcan to the statement he made this morning. I was glad to hear him make that statement, and I was pleased with most of what he said. It represents quite a change from what I can only describe as the sorry attitude of the government during the past two years toward matters of defence. I use those words advisedly, because the policy was apparently dictated by the idea that all people interested in the defence of the country must remain in complete uncertainty as to what they were supposed to do until the united nations had laid down some task for us to follow. In saying what he did the minister was adopting what we in this party have been advocating in every session since this parliament began. He said that the first job of the armed forces of Canada is to defend Canada. By saying that, the minister has put certainty into the purpose for which our armed forces exist, and I commend him for that statement. From now on we will have a chance to create an adequate defence force in this country and to keep it up through the years. It seems to me that at last the government is really coming to grips with defence problems and is getting its feet on the ground. I was so delighted with most of what the minister said that I can only

I want to refer in particular to only two of the minister's statements, although I think all fourteen of the points he brought out were good. First, he said that the purpose of the armed forces was to defend Canada, and, second, one of his fourteen long-term points was that there must be government leadership to get the Canadian people behind the armed forces of Canada. By making those statements he is hitting the nail squarely on the head, and I am heartened by their having been made.
I should like to say one word about what was said by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) who expressed the views of the C.C.F. party on defence matters. The statement he made was most interesting, because to me it showed that the socialists have not changed.
They have not.

The policy enunciated this afternoon by the hon. member, that we have no need of armed forces for internal security, that the first need of armed forces is to carry out some obligation imposed on us by a global organization, is just the disarmament talk of 1920 to 1940 dressed up in 1947 clothes. I warn the minister not to pay any attention to this disarmament policy. It was blown up before or by the last war. If he sticks to the policy which he has announced, which we in the Conservative party have urged on him, he will not go very far wrong.
I want to refer to one of the fourteen points announced by the minister, thait there is need for government leadership to get the support of the Canadian people and of all Canadian organizations behind the armed forces. I mention that point to underline its importance and I ask the minister to underline its importance throughout the country. He should lose no opportunity of enlisting the support of various civil organizations and individuals making up our national life. We are not a warlike people; we are inclined to wait until we get into trouble before we make these preparations. In the past the armed forces have been handicapped by a lack of public realization of their value. I do not think that attitude has changed much. The Minister of National Defence should always keep that idea in his mind and should prevent us from sinking back into the attitude we had between the wars.
The new certainty which he has given by his statement was badly needed by both the

active and the reserve forces. You cannot, as the minister has done, suddenly cut Canada's armed forces twenty-five per cent below what was stated to be the irreducible minimum without making people in the forces start to wonder whether the career they have chosen is worth while, and -whether the opportunities they thought were ahead of them before that change still remains. Today 'they will feel reassured that their future is a safe one. The minister's statement that provision is to. be made for permanent quarters for people in the active forces will do much to make these forces contented and of good morale. But when I turn to the reserve army-and I am dealing with the reserve army in particular, although I think it will apply to the reserve air force and to the reserve navy as well

I am not sure that the minister's statement today has really met their problem at all, at least not as far as it should.
The reserve army ought to have an honoured place in Canadian life. It should not be, as it is now and as it always has been, a poor relation of all other public functions. When the minister stated that the whole purpose of our force was to defend Canada, he might also have said.-and I think he will agree with me-that the reserve navy, army and air force are the first line of defence of Canada's shores and of the Canadian people. It is the reserve forces upon which we must rely in case we ever need to defend this country. The active force cannot possibly hope to provide more than an infinitesimal number of the force necessary. The minister should keep pounding on that idea when he goes around the country, and perhaps state the purpose of the Canadian forces, and particularly the reserve forces, more specifically even than he did today when he said that they were to. defend Canada. He should emphasize that the reserve forces are our first line of defence and are vitally necessary to us in these unfortunate and uncertain years. I do not think it can be said today that either the people of Canada or the reserve army itself feels that their purpose is so important in the mind of the government.
I took the trouble to find out from various parts of Canada how some chaps in whom I had considerable confidence were feeling about the reserve army of post-war days, and I was amazed at the uniform nature of the answers I received when I asked them how they were getting on. In every case it was said that the government had no certain policy. In other cases it was said that nobody had ever told them what their purpose was. In still other cases it was said that as a result of a failure to state the purpose and the policy behind the

Supply-National Defence
reserve forces recruits were not coming in, and the high morale with which a large number of excellent officers and N.C.O.'s entered the reserve army at the end of the war was not being maintained as well as they would have liked to see it. It is true that they had other complaints which are perhaps more difficult of solution, such as adequate training quarters. But the complete agreement of all these people right across Canada, from one end to the other, people who did not know each other, people who served in different parts of the country in different units and under completely different circumstances, is something which I do not think can be ignored.
While I commend, as I have said already, the minister on his statement today, I am bringing this point to his attention now because I say to him that we have had fine words but we have had no performance as yet. We are delighted to accept his words but we require a considerably higher measure of performance than has been provided by the department up until this year. I want to say to him. too, that there is a great deal of ground to be made up; that, as I understand the case, it is not as though he can now catch easily the spirit which existed in 1945. He has to go and dig for people, and give not only the units themselves and the officers and N.C.O.'s, but also the general public, the idea that he is behind his reserve army and that he proposes to make it good and popular and to bring it up to adequate strength; that he is going to provide both moral and material backing; and the most important of these is the moral backing which he alone in his capacity as Minister of National Defence can give. I told his predecessor last year that he could be the least expensive and the most effectual recruiting agency this country could possibly have.
I want to ask the minister to give us now, having stated his principles so excellently, a statement of the practical steps that he is proposing to take to stimulate interest in our reserve army. I want him to tell us its strength, to give us an idea of the average number of men on the strength in some typical units, to let us know how recruits are coming in, what the wastage is in the discharge of people who have joined and are now going out, and to give us some further information on this recruiting programme that he plans in September.
I also wish to say to him that for the reserve forces at least, a September recruiting programme will not do; that it has to be a continuous recruiting programme going on all the time, and recruits being provided not by a
campaign but by a continuous knowledge on the part of young people in each centre that in their armoury they can find interesting work, health-giving recreation, and above all that they have a useful part to play in Canada's service. I hope the minister will make a statement on the specific steps he proposes to take with respect to the reserve forces in carrying out these good principles that he has laid down.

I am glad to feel that I did not contribute anything to the heat of this afternoon. I shall try now to contribute something in the way of light upon the situation with regard to the reserve forces. I appreciate the kindly spirit of the remarks of previous speakers and t'heir very cooperative attitude, and1 I would like to deal with the question of reserves, because, as I have said on numerous occasions in this house and outsidie, they do form the foundation, the nucleus of any forces that might be needed to defend Canada in the event of an emergency.
I may tell the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, who took his seat a few minutes ago, that I have some first-hand experience of the work of the reserves because before going overseas in world war I, I was in a reserve infantry unit and upon returning I was in a a reserve artillery unit, and since then I have kept up the connection with that unit in Montreal. I can tell hon. members, as I believe many know, that immediately after the last war the reserves were in a very low condition indeed. For the year ended March 31, 1920-21, the sum of $1,160,000 was all that was provided for reserve training. In the unit in which I was, there was no equipment, there was very little training, there were a few officers and a few non-commissioned officers, there were very few men, and very soon interest diminished and it took years before the reserve was put on a proper footing. I believe that following this war we have taken steps to avoid that happening with regard to the reserve navy, the reserve army and the auxiliaries of the air force. First of all we have tried to create a new approach to the whole subject of reserves. Previously they were regarded as a rather special and frequently a social group who spent one or two days a week and sometimes some of their summer holidays in drill and1 some exercises. That was quite an improper attitude, but it was the attitude that was taken. Our view is that, the importance of the reserves having been shown in two wars, we should now take them for what they are, namely, an essential part of the armed forces of Canada, and that all differentiations between the active and the reserve should be wiped out. We have done it with regard to the navy by abolishing the wavy stripe. As far as possible it is done with regard to the army. Further, as far as possible officers, non-commissioned officers

Supply-National Defence
and men of the active and reserve forces mix together, wearing the same uniforms, undergoing the same training and using the same weapons. The psychological approach is therefore quite different.
With regard to the supply of training, there again we are on a different footing. New syllabuses, new methods of training developed during the war, are available, and every unit has full-time administrative and training personnel. This is an experiment that is being worked out in close cooperation with the reserve units themselves.
In addition, we aim to have in the reserve forces men who are physically fit and qualified from the military point of view to take their place in the field of action, should it become necessary, with a minimum of additional training. We believe that in many fields of activity it is possible over a longer period of time to bring the reserves up to the same efficiency as the active forces, and this year it seemed to us that the right place to start was first of all in getting these administrative and training officers attached to the various units and fitted into them; second, to have the units established through a cadre of officers and senior non-commissioned officers; and third, having them set up working conditions and administrative establishments that can really do the job when they get the men.
It would have been wrong for us to get large numbers of men without having officers, non-commissioned officers, training personnel and equipment to make really effective use of them so that they, in turn, would feel that they were making good use of their time. I believe from what I have seen, that in most units that have been activated across Canada, great progress has been made in these preliminary steps of organization. To indicate something of the magnitude of the difference between the reserve army now and what is was before the war, or still more at the end of the last war, I might mention that the amount provided in the army estimates alone for the reserve forces is of the order of $13 million. That is a sum equivalent to the total provided in the year 193233 for all the armed forces of Canada put together. But that is only part of the picture, because a major part of the work of the active forces is the training of the reserve and the supplying of stores, equipment and motor vehicles for them. This is now being done on a scale quite different from anything which has been done in the past.
With regard to numbers, the total number in the reserve army at June 15 was 33,704 men, to which should be added, I think, 1.418 in the Canadian officers training corps, although they
do not form part of the reserve properly so-called. That makes a total of 35,122 men. For those on the establishment, training is provided this year for thirty days; and in addition, 10,000 are to receive fourteen days' training at summer camps. Provision is made to give 15,000 tradesmen and specialists, if they are available, fifteen days' additional training at local headquarters.
How many of those are officers and non-commissioned officers?
Of the 33,704, there are 4,716 officers.

Can the minister say among how many units that total is divided?
Mr. CLAXTQN; I have not the figures.
Has the minister a rough idea?

I will see if I can give it. It would be misleading to give any total number of units, because they vary from units which exist only as names on paper in the total establishment provided for, to units which are over their established strength; hence any notion of the number of units would be quite misleading. But there are approximately 650 units active in the reserve army in Canada.

Could the minister give a rough average of the number who would be on the strength of an infantry battalion, an artillery regiment, and field company engineers, so that we would have some idea of whether a unit existed on paper only or was one sufficient to train.

The fact that there are 35,122 officers and men on the strength indicates that there is a substantial group of officers and men on the strength. However, I will try to get for my hon. friend some indication of the kind he has requested.
That is not as many as there were before the war, is it?
Oh, no. Before the war there were about 45,000, according to my recollection.
That is correct.
Then, before the war I think the largest number to receive annual training at camp was about 14,000.
Seventeen thousand in 1938.

This year we hope that an equal number will receive a superior type of training at camp.

Now with regard to recruits: there are exceptions, but in the great number of units that I have seen it would not have been a good thing for those units to have more recruits than they have at the present time. Their state of organization, the state of the equipment and training must be put into good order before they are ready to handle recruits properly. In some units that is not so. I have no doubt that with a campaign such as we envisage taking place towards the end of the summer, we can obtain for the reserve army the recruits that are needed to fill up whatever is fixed for their establishment for the next training year. I think that result will follow very easily for the great majority of units.
The hon. member has rather flatteringly urged that more attention be paid by myself, in my speeches, to the reserves. I have done what I could, I must say, on four occasions in the house so far, and I think in speeches in every province in Canada, including the four western provinces; certainly in a large number of speeches. I have not only endeavoured to draw the attention of the communities to the importance of the reserve, but also I have met reserve officers and men of the navy, army and air force at meetings specially arranged, and have discussed frankly with them the plans we have for them. Also I should say that I have met representatives of the council of defence of the reserve associations of the army-there are some eleven of them-representatives of the associations of the naval and air force officers in various parts of the country, and discussed frankly with them arrangements for reserve training and ways and means whereby we can work together in order to do this important job. I must say that the response has been good, and I believe that with the support of hon. members and other leaders in the community we can really make progress in this field.
I wish to say one word in conclusion on that subject, and it is this. In t'he western command there has been established a practice which has been found most useful. Under Major General Worthington there has been set up in each reserve unit in the western command a civilian committee charged with the function of supporting that unit in every way possible. In the great majority of cases these civilian committees are doing useful work in support of the reserve units. We hope that- the same procedure will be applied in other commands across Canada. I may tell hon. members that as part of the changed organization of the armed forces, general officers commanding commands, and there are IMr. Claxton.]
five of them across Canada, are given very much greater authority than ever before on a decentralized basis, and for the first time they can say what units are ready to take what classes of training. If a unit is ready to take training to a greater extent than is provided in the quota, he has power to make the necessary adjustments. Also the per capita grant made to the officers commanding units is to be on a flexible basis for the first time, so it can be adjusted by the general officer commanding. These arrangements have been made pursuant to suggestions by the reserve associations, and they have met with very general support. I would say our expectation is that the reserve units will be established on a very sound basis by the time they begin their autumn training this year.

If I may follow up what the minister has just said, I simply want to repeat that according to my information the men are not coming into the reserve army. I ask the minister to take that as an honest statement of opinion after investigation and look into this question again. Then I want to ask him this question. When the reserve army was first formed mj'- understanding is that its total strength was to be 180,000, and that it was on a six-divisional basis. Since that time it has been cut, along with the regular forces, by two-thirds, according to a press report I have here. This would mean it was cut to about 50,000 men. Were the units in the reserve army, that is the divisions and the individual units, cut at the same time, or did that cut of two-thirds mean that an infantry battalion, for instance, would be authorized to train only one-third its proper strength, and so on with other units? From my own experience in the non-permanent militia before the war I feel quite certain that if you authorize the training by a unit of only one-third its strength, or perhaps even less, and only pay it for that number of men on strength, you will do quite a lot of damage to the reserve army, even without intending to do so. If the minister is going to cut the total force envisaged I think it very important that he cut the number of units instead of cutting the number of men who can be trained in a unit.

The newspaper report to which the hon. gentleman has referred of course is quite wrong. There is nothing whatever in it. There was no justification and no basis for it. The establishment of the reserve forces of Canada remains exactly as it was, and no change has been announced in that.

It remains at 150,000?

Supply-National Defence

It stands at 180,000 plus, and that is about what it was before the war. There have been adjustments to bring the figure into line with changes in the types of arms, and changes in the population of Canada, but there has been no great change in the figure of 180,000 as compared with what it was before the war. That is the establishment which has been set down on paper for six divisions, should it ever be decided to raise six divisions in the event of a war. However, it was never planned by anyone that there should be 180,000 officers and men in the reserve army of Canada in peace time, or if that was planned I never heard of it. The figure generally set has been of the magnitude of 50,000, or something of that kind; and for this year the ceiling was set at
30,000.	We have exceeded that, as I have indicated, by some three or four thousand; and the figure for training will be set early next year so the officers commanding units may know what the programme is. We are combining that with what my hon. friend suggested; that is, leaving units dormant, on paper, rather than activating them when there seems very little chance of getting them up to strength and efficiency. The greatest possible attention is being paid to units in centres having quarters, equipment and traditions which indicate the strong probability of their being successfully brought to a state of efficiency at an early date.

I listened with great interest this morning to the comprehensive review of his department given by the minister. While it took some time to present that statement I think it was well worth while. I believe it was one of the most informative statements we have had from a minister of national defence in recent years.
I rise at this time to obtain some information from the minister. Recently in this city we had the opportunity to witness a parade of uniformed corps, under the discipline of officers and non-commissioned' officers, bearing arms. Some of us judge there were between 2,500 and 3,000 men in these units. Large numbers of them carried, rifles which were issued to the French army in the war of 1914-18. A smaller number carried Lee Enfield service rifles of the most recent issue, and some carried swords of a cavalry type. While I and others associated' with me were enjoying the martial music and the rather gorgeous and unusual uniforms and admiring the military appearance of these corps, we were wondering what section of the Canadian armed forces w'e were seeing march by, because most of us had not been in eastern Canada for very long. Therefore I would like to ask the
minister this question. Are these corps, which were under the discipline of officers and noncommissioned officers and bearing arms, under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence? If they are not, is it safe for us then to assume that there is nothing in the Militia Act or the law of this country or any regulation that prevents any organization from training uniformed men in corps under the discipline of officers and non-commissioned officers, and bearing arms?

I must say I did not see the officers and men to whom the hon. gentleman has referred, so I am not in a position to speak about them at first hand. I recognize that he has had a very gallant war record and a great deal of experience and that he is in a position to speak at first hand, so I take it that what he says is correct. I must say it surprises me very much to hear that these forces, which I should think were quite outside the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence, had anything in the nature of Lee Enfield service rifles. We have not disposed of any rifles in Canada except to some of the Pacific Coast Rangers, and they received American sporting rifles, not the service Lee Enfields. I do not know of any other rifles that have been disposed of to civilian corps or organizations in Canada. I shall be very glad to look into the question and also to look into the question of law to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

We have had some discussion of the navy estimates, and also some discussion of the army and the reserve army. I should like now to draw the attention of the minister and the committee to the air force. But before doing so may I answer an observation by the hon. member for Regina City, who asked how it was that our citizen army did not lose the last war and how it had time to mobilize. May I tell him that it was the air force that gave the army time to mobilize, and that is why I wish to speak on the air force today. If the hon. member thinks that anyone in any government in Canada has any idea of aggressive warfare his thought is complete proof of his absolute military ignorance, and all that he has said on defence should therefore be treated with the contempt it deserves.
I hope the hon. gentleman will not attempt to put words into my mouth. I can express myself volubly and adequately without any assistance from my excellent friend.

You asked how a citizen army won the last war, and I am telling you.

Turning to the minister's statement of this morning, I was delighted to hear him place on the record of this house the war records of all the Canadian services. I am sure that we were delighted to see that the government have at last an appreciation of what the aims of the defence forces should be and that they have also a plan of action, which I should like brieffy to discuss.	[DOT]
This fourteen point plan has already been referred to. In my opinion it is very domestic in nature. First the minister speaks of the unification of the departments, then of joint intelligence and planning. I feel that the intelligence side of it is important. The planning should be well on its way now; the department has had two years at least in which to consider its plans. Then the minister spoke of an appreciation of the factors in the last war. I happen to know a little bit about this subject, and whether Canada has an appreciation of it or not I would like to inform the minister that the military appreciations of most other fighting nations on the democratic side were arrived at before this war was over.
The fourth point speaks of active and reserve qualified officers-again domestic in its'nature. When we get to the seventh point we begin to get something which seems to me important; it has to do with adequate reserves of equipment and weapons. It was amply proved in the last war that the degree of technology required to equip adequately any fighting service was of growing and tremendous importance. This seventh point seems to me to be the only really important one up to this stage. The eighth point deals with the integration of the armed forces, the ninth with cooperation with industry, and the tenth with Canadian Arsenals Limited, and with the design and manufacture of munitions, etc. If we intend to design and manufacture munitions in Canada it will be necessary for the government to give certain contracts both to our industrial organization and to Canadian Arsenals Limited. It will be necessary in those contracts to lay down sendee specifications which will keep our arms up to date, instead of letting them get out of date as we have done in many cases heretofore.
Then there is civilian defence and government leadership. The same government leadership that we asked for two or three years ago is now on the fourteen point programme. It is heartening to see it there and I must congratulate the new minister on his recognition of this necessity. It is indeed a step foiward, though it comes at a rather late date.

Point thirteen deals with commercial cooperation and point fourteen with cooperation with the commonwealth and other friendly democratic nations not inclined towards aggression but inclined to stand and fight for their country.
I said at the outset that I wished to refer particularly to the air force. It seemed to me at the end of the war that the job which the air forces of all the nations did actually spoke for itself, and I thought it would not be necessary to speak on behalf of the air force in this house at least, because it was so evident in every action that we fought successfully in the last war that the air was the dominant factor. However, the rats have been gnawing at the policies of the government since the war, and I feel that it is necessary for me here today to remind the Minister of National Defence and the government that they are behind the times with regard to Canada's air defence, so deplorably behind the times that I am actually shocked when I read the answers that were brought down for me on the fifty-eighth day of this session in reply to seven questions that I had asked. I call attention particularly to one thing. We find that the strength of headquarters establishment is over double the actual number of men who should be there. In other words in non-effective jobs, in non-operational functions, there are over double the number of men who should be used on this particular type of work.
We have heard earlier of the auxiliary and reserve forces being the backbone of our defence system. The government authorized fifteen auxiliary squadrons to be established and equipped across Canada. I understand that six of these squadrons have actually been established, that four are in process of establishment, and that five have been deferred indefinitely. I shall not discuss their equipment.	The minister knows what kind of
equipment they have and what sort of shape it is in, and I am sure he is not awfully proud of it.
Just why the government has failed to establish auxiliary squadrons at Halifax and Victoria is very difficult to understand. Halifax, as the minister well knows, was one of our key defensive sites in this war, with a fine harbour, aerial headquarters for the north Atlantic convoy patrol, and equipped also with excellent fighter defence. Why we should not have had an auxiliary squadron established at Halifax, which is our key winter port, is difficult to understand. It is equally difficult to understand why an auxiliary squadron should not have been established at Victoria. Ottawa

could have been left out for a while, because after all there are so many airmen here at headquarters that perhaps they could defend us without an auxiliary squadron. We find also that no auxiliary squadron is established at Calgary and Quebec. In my opinion the fight for recognition of the auxiliary air force must begin all over again. It seems to me that here in Canada our air force has been pushed into the background until today it is actually but a shadow of its former self.
I would not take up this fight today if I were not sure that the defence of Canada is tied completely to our air strength. I speak only of defence; I speak only of the repelling of an aggressor. It was that same air strength that gave Britain her time in 1940, and it is that same air strength which can stop any aggressor flying over our country and rendering us helpless in something like sixty days, which people now predict is all that would be required to knock out a modern industrial power. If we take those sixty days into consideration we realize that we would not have time to prepare our air defences after there has been a declaration or indication of war. Those air defences must be prepared now. So that the minister may not think I am extreme in asking him to prepare the air defences now, I should like to quote an article from the Letter Review of June 30, 1947, with reference to statements made by Colonel Goforth:
We have perhaps ten years of comparative safety from attack, perhaps followed by another five or ten years of rather acute danger, after which, if war has not occurred, the odds against it will become definitely better.
Colonel Goforth says that we have perhaps ten years of comparative safety. His opinion is not altogether agreed with by a presidential commission in the United States, which is referred to in a report in the Globe and Mail of June 2, 1947. The question was asked:	When should such an attack be
expected? This is the reply of the commission :
For a period estimated by responsible scientists at not less than four years and not more than ten years, we can expect immunity from such an attack because we alone possess the atomic bomb.
That commission in Washington gives the United States four years of immunity. They said earlier in their report that the possibilities of an atomic age war are so great and the destruction would be so ferocious that it would require sixty days or less to determine whether the United States would win or lose. We have a Canadian authority saying we have ten years of immunity and a United States authority saying we have only four
years of immunity. They are referring to a war fought with the same weapons we used in the last war; but a lot of people are concerned with a push button war. A report in the Globe and Mail of April 10 quoting a dispatch from Washington states that it will be at least twenty-five years before an atomic rocket war is possible.
I am laying the position before the government that there is an immunity of from four to ten years, with the possibility that a rocket war is twenty-five years away. The government have the defence of Canada in their hands. What are they going to do about it? Are they going to build drill halls and dig a few trenches here and there, or are they going to be realistic? Are they going to face the problem and say, "How can we defend Canada; how can we repel an aggressor?" I think the only answer that can be given is that an interceptor air force must be built up.
Lest the minister should think that I am merely expressing my own opinion with regard to the functions of the air force I would refer him to Sir Arthur Harris, who is reported in the Globe and Mail of April 26, 1947, as follows:
He said he "supposed" the invasion of Germany was carried out because "we had the troops to invade with," but insisted air power could have done the job alone.
I emphasize that word "alone". There is also a report made in October, 1945, by the D'Olier civilian commission, and in this connection I quote from the New York Times of October 31, 1945, as follows:
A civilian committee, after an exhaustive survey of the air war in Europe, declared today that, while allied air power was "decisive" in forcing Germany's defeat, a number of phases of the strategic bombing campaign were ineffective in their long range results.
I just call the minister's attention to the fact that that is the report of a civilian commission. They declared that the allied air power was decisive. I want also to refer to German military experts. This is the opinion of one of the enemy who felt the weight of our air force in the war. He said:
Your bombing of our communications prevented our troops from ever coming into effective tactical employment against your forces. Without this strategic bombing the invasion would have been a dismal failure.
I regret that I cannot give the name of the German expert as that is taken from the speech delivered by Sir Arthur Harris in Montreal. He quoted another German expert as saying:
We had forty reserve divisions in readiness. Your bombing made it impossible to move our troops rapidly, if at all,

But we also know well that you are always ready to bring your mighty effort closer in when such action is really needed and to cooperate in our tactical battle. When you do this your action is always decisive.

In the past in Great Britain and also in the United States there was a fight for recognition of the air force. In Great Britain Lord Trenchard fought for recognition and understanding of the air force. In the United States the great General Billy Mitchell's words and predictions were well borne out in this war. In Canada great men like Bishop, Barker and others carried on the same fight. We also had the premier of Ontario, Colonel George Drew, an artillery man who wrote that great volume "'Canada's Fighting Airmen". Somehow between the first and the second war the job that the airmen, did was forgotten or not properly appreciated. It is my desire today to bring these facts to the attention of the government to see whether they really intend to carry out the first aim that the minister expressed when he said the aim was to defend Canada, because if he wants to defend Canada he must make the same decision today that Great Britain made in 1936 when they started to build up their fighter forces. They Started to build up these fighter forces in preparation for what they knew would happen should a war develop. They chose to build their defensive forces. I speak .today not of anything in the way of aggression as far as the air force is concerned. I speak only of defence so that my socialist friends cannot misinterpret anything I say. All I want to do is to defend Canada. I do not want to strike anyone else, or do anything like that. I am merely pointing out. that the way to defend Canada is the same way that Britain defended the British isles in 1940. If the minister is sincere in his first aim, then he must get his air force on an effective operational basis and see that it is properly equipped and manned by sufficient people at least to repel the majority of any invading air force that may stand prepared to attack our country.

From the United Kingdom.

We have experimental
work going on with both planes and jet engines. The situation is as I have described it. We have weapons that were used in the last war. We are going to get aeroplanes that may be useful in some future war, when we can get them, but we cannot get them unless they are being produced, and unfortunately the production does not lie within our own hands; it lies within the hands, of another country.
With regard to our ignoring the air force, as the hon. member seemed to indicate, I think

Men with remarkable flying and fighting records. I visited some of them at the air staff college. I remember saying to the commanding officer, Air Commodore Ross, G.C., as I left: "These are a magnificent group of men," and he said: "Yes, sir, I do

I have advocated that we equip our air force with modern weapons for the npxt four to ten years. When General Doolittle and the others made their statement they were looking into the future.
Mr. CLAXTO'N: I do not necessarily agree with them. I quote them to show that there are two extreme points of view.

I am glad that the minister takes a realistic attitude on the problem of defence. Speaking in Halifax on June 24 he is reported to have said that Canada considers that peace must be based on understanding and knowledge, and meanwhile she, meaning Canada, meant to see there is nothing second-rate about her navy, her army or her air force. I agree whole-heartedly with that attitude, and the minister is to be congratulated on it.
I rose to say a word about another matter and that is the wearing of military dress in peace time by officers and men in Canada's permanent services. What sort of defence shall we have when irresponsible attacks on officers force them to abandon the wearing of their uniforms for fear they may be called "brass hats" or something of the kind? I go on now to the important matter of training. The chief of the general staff, speaking of university cadets and junior officer training, according to a report in the Calgary Herald said that, after serving for three months a year for three years, such officers would1 be well trained in the most modem weapons. Well, in my opinion there months a year for three years will not adequately train an officer in the most modern weapons. I doubt whether three years of intensive training will bring an officer up to high efficiency in the most modern weapons. Every day, every month, every year we are getting more complicated weapons. More and more do we need engineering scientific and technical skill. To say you can train a man for three months, then send him back to his civilian occupation for nine months, then start training him again, and carry this on for three years, and that at the end of three years you will have an efficient officer capable of instructing others is in my opinion, not a correct statement of fact. I am not being critical of what has been said because, as I indicated, this is merely a newspaper report; but I want to show that with the present highly intricate, extremely technical and high speed methods of warfare it is infinitely more important now than ever before that those in our fighting forces should receive the highest and most intense type of training. We cannot allow ourselves to get into the position in which we found ourselves in 1939. We can never take that risk again. Whether it is a push-button war or a war on the surface of the tundras, no matter what it is we must have our intelligence giving us proper and complete information; and we must be prepared at least 
to repel the first attack before it reaches the centres of population. One thing is absolutely sure, the speed of warfare is constantly accelerating, and the range, accuracy and destructive power of all weapons are increasing tremendously.

The hon. member referred to an article in the Calgary Herald of July 3 which reports Lieutenant General Foulkes, chief of the general staff, as rejecting the possibility of a push-button war occurring in the immediate future and calling it poppycock. If that is what the chief of the general staff said I must say he made the statement on the best authority, because on July 2 Field-Marshal Viscount Montgomery said at a press conference there was no evidence yet of a future war of the push-button variety. It seems to me that the chief of the general staff was speaking with the best possible authority and also with good sense. There has been a great deal of talk about push-button wars as well as about saucers flying in formation and the like. That does not mean that we should not keep up to date and do the utmost in research and industrial organization and have as much as we can afford of the most modern weapons. But it does seem to me that we should keep our feet on the ground and look at the realities and consider what the probabilities are in the light of the best kind of intelligence we can get. I am sure that the chief of the general staff in speaking as he did was endeavouring to meet this extreme kind of excited and unrealistic statement which is doing a good deal at the present time to upset the world and effect the chances of our working out some foundation for living together.
I should also like to say this. The chief of the general staff and, I must say, all the other officers of the armed forces with hardly a single exception have, since I have been there, been scrupulously careful to speak only on matters that would properly come within their fields. Sometimes they are quoted when they do not expect to be, and sometimes they have been misquoted, but I want to say at once that there has been nothing but the most loyal cooperation in what I believe every hon. member would regard as the best kind of parliamentary as well as service practice.

The minister has, in my judgment, impressed the house with his sincerity and his realistic approach to the problems of his high office, and I wish to congratulate him on his approach and on the way in which he is attacking his problems. The social crediters he will find will endeavour to take a realistic attitude toward Canada's defence as they have done since first coming into public life. In 1936 I made a statement supporting the immediate preparation by Canada for effective participation in the war before ever I came into parliament. Social crediters have taken the attitude consistently, that we should be prepared. It will be altogether too late if we are caught unprepared. One of the speakers referred to the miraculous way in which we came out of the last war with everything against us, seeming, I thought, to imply that we need not now worry too much about being prepared, that we shall come out of the next war in a similar way. That reasoning is probably satisfactory if one does not carry it too far. But what came into my mind as he spoke was: How far and how often should we tempt Providence? Our coming out of the last war successfully was, I think, the result of a great many miraculous interventions by Providence by which we were enabled to save ourselves when our own management did not justify us in expecting to come out of that war successfully at all.
The minister's words have a pleasing and reassuring sound, as most hon. members have pointed out to the committee. All will depend upon the interpretation which he and his department place upon his words, and also upon the attitude which the people of Canada adopt towards defence matters. I thought the remark made by the hon. member for Vegre-ville concerning silly remarks made about brass hats and the effect that they had on certain gentlemen in the country were very appropriate. In any democracy such as Canada, comprising peoples of different racial origins and with four parties participating in Canadian political life, the greatest care must be exercised by everybody who expresses himself in public or in private, whether it be through the press or otherwise, because so frequently what is said has effects which were not intended.

In a general way I am somewhat concerned about the substantial cuts which have been made in these defence estimates. The minister has said nothing either privately or publicly to indicate that t3ie treasury board were hard on him. If they were, probably the first thing we shall have to do is to assure the treasury board that we do not want the defence needs of Canada to be controlled by the treasury board. We want the treasury board to be controlled by the defence needs of Canada. I think the minister should assert himself definitely in this respect. I gathered from his words that he had in mind the defence we could afford rather more than the defence we needed. I think he should determine the kind of defence we need in Canada and then, having determined that, tell this parliament how much money this is going to cost and require parliament to vote the money. That may sound a little extreme. But if we got into war we would not hesitate regarding money. We would give the minister a blank cheque just as we did in the last war. Why not give him a blank cheque while we are preparing for war? That seems the sensible thing, and that is the policy that, I with moderation, would advocate that parliament should adopt with respect to defence.
I believe the minister ought to inform parliament from time to time as to Canada's needs so that he can take us into his confidence. We shall trust that there will come into parliament no members who will be as irresponsible as a number of members were before the last war, and who will say things that never should be said to the minister. I trust we shall all be able to keep our feet on the ground, all political parties and all racial extractions' all over Canada, so that we shall have the best chance of coming through these perilous times we face with the best possible hope of coming out successfully, so that our children and our grandchildren and future generations may continue to enjoy the freedom which our race has struggled: for through the centuries.
Canada should, I believe, assume that her defence will depend, of course, upon her own efforts, but mainly upon the efforts of the British commonwealth and empire as a whole. Our friends in the commonwealth and empire have always been ready in the past, and there is no reason why they should not be ready in the times to come. Twice within the memory of all of us we have faced what seemed to be an impossible situation. The British commonwealth has proved to be the backbone, the stomach and the sinews which saved us, under God, in both those wars. I
