think we would be well advised to assume that similar conditions will obtain in the future.
Canada should look very carefully to the British commonwealth and empire. I suggest to the minister that we should endeavour to build up that commonwealth and empire, so that it will possess the industrial strength which is necessary to fight a major war. To defend ourselves in such terrible ' times, we must have industrial self-sufficiency.
I would direct the attention of the minister to what Canada has done in providing herself with rubber through the Polymer establishment. It would be well if Canada would see that every major necessity which it is possible to provide is provided, including large supplies of vital commodities. Every member of the commonwealth should follow the same policy, so that we shall not be in danger of being emasculated, by being cut in two or probably in four through the exigencies of a future [DOT]war. There should be the greatest cooperation among the members of the commonwealth and the empire in all matters pertaining to the economic and financial strength of the empire.
I think we should strive to build up morale in the commonwealth. We should bring about such conditions in our commonwealth that we shall have prosperity and a high standard of living, so much so that the people will know that the commonwealth is a good place in which to live. We have a good illustration of what might happen if such conditions do not obtain. I think it is well known that the main reason why Eire diid not fight in the last war was that conditions economically in Eire had been allowed to deteriorate below a reasonable standard. Eire made up her mind that she simply had to be independent in order to have a greater measure of prosperity. There is no reason why Eire should not be more prosperous as an integral part of the British commonwealth than she could possibly be alone. There have been faulty policies adopted throughout the empire which have resulted in Eire feeling that she had to go out of the empire. People are much inclined to look at the standards of living which they have when they are estimating the value of conditions under which they live. I say that we should raise commonwealth morale by bringing about high standards of prosperity in every part of the empire.
This may all seem a little off the subject of defence, but we must bear in mind that in times of war there is a good deal of truth in what was said regarding the contestants in world war I. It was said that that war would be won by the nation with the deepest stock-

ing; in other words, by the nation that had the strongest financial resources. We should keep in mind that we simply must keep ourselves economically strong all over the empire; otherwise we are not going to fight successfully. Let me mention to the minister, in passing that there has been a dietermined attempt on the part of a nation that should know better, to break down imperial preferences in the British commonwealth, thereby weakening the economic structure of all the members of the commonwealth. Such attempts as that should be resisted with every bit of strength that we can muster, both publicly and in private, until everybody comes to realize that we mus,t insist on safeguarding our economic and financial strength as a part of our preparations for defence. Imperial preference is one of the devices which we have found advantageous in the past in the development of our financial and economic strength, and obviously it will be a device of great value in that respect in the future.
There should be financial cooperation among the members of the commonwealth to obtain expansion of production and consumption. There should be adopted a scientific method of distribution, both domestically and throughout the commonwealth. I do not propose to enter into a discussion of what method should be used, but I do say that nothing has been found up to the present time that begins to compare in theory with the social credit proposals. If social credit were applied throughout the British commonwealth and empire the empire's fighting strength would be astoundingly increased. It would enable all parts of the empire to take advantage of the resources of all the empire, a thing which today is quite impossible. I point that out to the minister; I point that out to the members of the house and to the people of the country who will read my words.
Up to the present it has not been a question of the capacity of the various members of the empire to produce; it has not been a question of the resources they have; it has been a question of whether we can use those resources. In the past, except in times of war, we have not been able to use the valuable resources which Providence has put in our hands. Let any man who thinks he is able to devise a way of solving the problem proceed immediately to offer his suggestion. I suggest that the application of social credit is a means at our disposal which would make us strong for the terrible times which I think every member in this house feels are not very far ahead.

After the commonwealth, Canada should count upon the United States. I think the minister is doing that quite satisfactorily. There is no objection to close cooperation and collaboration with the United States, but in our dealings with the United States we should be sure that we are protecting our interests politically, economically, financially and strategically. It may not be entirely in order for a member of the Canadian House of Commons to make observations concerning the transfer of so many of our commonwealth bases for forty or fifty outmoded ships during the last war, but I think every red-blooded Britisher from one end of the empire to the other resented deeply the fact that the United States took advantage of the difficulties we were in to get 99-year leases on certain vital bases in the British commonwealth. When we consider that her own safety was at stake just as much as ours, I think we must all agree that the correct words to use about that occurrence would not be suitable words to use in a parliament of the empire.
So I say we ought to take pains to see to it that we protect ourselves politically, economically, financially and strategically before the next war, during the next war and after the next war whenever we are dealing with the United States. I have no desire to be harsh about things which happened during the last six or seven years. We are grateful for the assistance that the United States gave us, but I hope she is equally grateful for the assistance we have given her.
Canada should not neglect the united nations organization, but we should be very careful with respect to that organization. Of course most hon. members are quite at variance with me in regard to that organization, but I think the day will come when they will see things very much as I see them in respect of the whole united nations organization and the charter. I would warn that we do not trust too far in our dealings with that organization. We should take every care to guard our sovereignty and freedom, politically, economically, financially and strategically, just as we should with respect to the United States before the coming war, during the war and after the war.
All we need to do is to remember the dismal record of the league of nations. There are those who will say, "Well, the united nations organization is quite different from the league of nations." I do not see that it is any more likely to succeed than the league of nations was. Hon. members know what happened to
us as the result of the league of nations. I was as ardent an advocate of the league of nations as anyone, but this is what actually occurred. The league of nations caused the British commonwealth to count upon it too much. It caused us to neglect our defences in every way. It even made it so that it was difficult to get an intelligent and realistic discussion in the matter of defence in the various houses of parliament of the empire. If anything like that occurs as a result of the united nations-and we see signs of that already- then the united nations organization can be something that we may regret very deeply. Therefore I say, let us just be careful in respect of that organization. I am afraid it will be found by the people of the future that the whole united nations organization and united nations covenant were devised as a LTnited States commercial contrivance, aimed at increasing the sales of United States goods all over the world. That was the primary object.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have allowed the hon. memher wide latitude, but I feel that he should direct his remarks to the department which is being considered, the Department of National Defence. I realize that there is some connection between economic theories and defence, but I do not think the estimates of the department should be used to illustrate economic theories. May I ask the hon. member to confine his remarks more directiy to national defence.

I have said all I want to say in that respect, Mr. Chairman, but I think it would be quite in order to point out to you and to hon. members that whenever we have endeavoured to bring these matters up before the House of Commons they have been always out of order on one ground or another. Yet it can be found that these matters are of the most vital concern to us. There is something radically wrong in the world today; otherwise we should not have a world divided into two great camps, led by two great nations, each of which prides itself upon being a peace-loving nation. There is something terribly wrong somewhere. We ought to find out what is the matter, but I will say no more on this now. I would simply say that the nations would be well advised to be wary how far they put their trust in the united nations organization for their defence.
In my judgment steps ought to be taken to have the people of Canada informed as fully as possible on all matters pertaining to Canadian defence. The value of the British commonwealth, the greatness, the strength, the
Supply-National Defence

potentialities of the British commonwealth should be brought before the people. In centres throughout the country, in the press and elsewhere, I find a tendency nowadays to disregard these matters. I was principal of schools for some twenty years before I entered parliament. I know what was on the curriculum of the schools in Alberta. I think Alberta was no different in this regard from the other provinces. The attention which has been given to these vital matters of our defence has been so slight that the boys and girls have had no chance at all to form a sound opinion as to how to plot their course for the greatest possible safety of their society. How you can possibly have a nation safe when it is so ill-informed on vital matters is something that I fail to be able to see. What I suggest to the minister is that a part of his work should be devising ways and means whereby we can get out to the youth of this country and the people generally the essential facts. The remarks of the hon. member for York West regarding intelligence were appropriate. I would take the matter of intelligence just a little bit further and advise that intelligence for the people all over the country concerning all matters pertaining to the national well-being and defence should be more carefully attended to. Every precaution should be taken to see that nothing but the absolute truth is given. That is a matter which would help us greatly in our defence in the future.
Much attention ought to be given to the causes of war and how to remove them. In his statement this morning, the minister said nothing as to the causes of wrar or whether or not we are doing anything to remove them. I would think that if we want to defend ourselves one of the very first things we ought to discover is whether or not we are contributing to the causes of the next world war by the policies which we are pursuing. I think there is hardly any doubt that we are contributing to the causes of the next war by the policies we are pursuing. In my opinion, much attention should be given to that by the minister. Let it be borne in mind that the cause of war is hot commercial rivalry, the struggle for markets and for raw material; also unemployment and poverty which brings about such extreme movements as the nazi movement and other movements which indirectly resulted in the last war. To what extent are we pursuing policies which are resulting in the accomplishment of the evils from which we suffered in the last war? In my judgment, much could be done to eliminate or at least to remove the intensity of the struggle for markets and raw 
materials. It seems to me that the minister is partly responsible for discovering what that may be and advocating that it ought to be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not think the Minister of National Defence, as Minister of National Defence, has any control over the discovery of markets. I do not think that discussion should be carried on under these estimates.

As a matter of fact, it is a matter of difference of opinion. The minister is meeting -with the other members of the cabinet and the cabinet is devising the policy for this country. However I am not going to pursue the matter. I submit to the minister that he seriously consider it just as other hon. members should.
The citizens of Canada ought to be trained in first aid of all kinds. In his statement, the minister hardly mentioned that. Possibly he has something of that sort in mind, but we Should not wait until the V-l and the V-2 bombs and the other horrible monstrosities come, to begin to teach our people first aid. The people should know all about these things. They should have first-aid shelters all over the country. I had the privilege of being in Britain in 1941 along with the Chairman. He will remember how difficult it had been for them to establish first-aid shelters and how important they were. I should think they ought to be established all over the country before the trouble comes along. Why should people not be trained? I should think it would be a part of our defence mechanism.
We should have people trained in firefighting, because certainly if any credence can be placed in the suggestions as to what terrible instruments of war are being developed, fire is going to play an important part in the suffering which people have to go through in the next war. Fire will be among the people just as it was in Britain.
There should be an organization for local defence. The minister has talked about reserves. I would commend him for all he said about keeping up the reserve force, but I have an idea that the people should be trained as citizens' armies. I remember the great anxiety which wras felt in certain parts of Canada when we were in the midst of danger from attack by the Japanese. I heard people in western areas say they would give almost anything if they had a few machine guns and knew how to use them, because the possession of the right kind of arms, and skill in using them, by the ordinary citizen, by farmers and others who might be in danger of being overrun, could easily have turned the

Supply-National Defence
tide in ease of a Japanese invasion. This matter should be given a great deal of thought while we are training reserve forces. I may have more to say regarding defence at a later time, but perhaps this is sufficient for the present.

During this debate we have heard many speeches about the navy, the army and the air force, and I feel that I should say a few words at this time. I cannot be accused of taking up much of the time of the house. As a matter of fact, this is only the third time I have risen to speak. I hear certain murmurs on the other side of the house but I ignore them. I could discuss the army and perhaps do so sensibly since I was a member of the southern Alberta regiment for three years, but I will not go into that question at the present time. I intend to discuss it under another item, particularly with regard to the uniforms that men in the army have to wear. I have worn these uniforms, and when I put them on I certainly did not feel very well dressed in comparison with members of the air force and the navy.. I intend to go into that question under the appropriate item when we come to it.
The matter I now wish to discuss does not pertain to any of the three services. I am not sure where I am in order, thought I hope I am. If not, then I can discuss it under some other item. What I shall have to say now has reference to the area that is known as the British block adjoining Medicine Hat. It is an area that was taken over in 1941 by the Department of National Defence, and this meant the moving of 130 families from the area.
The area comprises 700,000 acres of land. Last January, at the convention of the united farmers of Alberta a resolution was passed unanimously endorsing steps taken by one of the men who were moved from that area. In the course of this session every hon. member must, I am sure, have received a copy of the resolution. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee _ in reading the resolution now, since, as I say, everyone has a copy of it. The minister, I believe, also received a copy. The resolution was passed, as I say, at a convention of the united farmers of Alberta, which is the largest organization of farmers in that province, and it was passed unanimously.
On March 15, 1947, there appeared in Maclean's magazine an article under the title "Cross Country", from which I will read
certain excerpts for the information of hon. members. This is what the writer of this article states:
In the dark wartime spring of 19411 a party representing the British government appeared in the "British block" of southern Alberta, a sparsely settled area of more than 700,000 acres between Suffield and the Saskatchewan boundary. They wanted the land, and they wanted it fast.
To each of the 130 families in the block this offer was made: trade acre for acre, for crown lands north of the Red Deer river, plus a cash settlement for buildings, or, instead, a straight $6.50 per acre. The farmers thought both offers unfair.
But the government-and the war-couldn't wait. R.C.M.P. officers summoned the farmers to court in Medicine Hat, where they were summarily ordered off their land in 15 days, and recompensed at $1 an acre for raw land, five cents per acre for each unexpired year on leased land, and $4 per acre for standing crops, $2 per head for moving livestock and no stated offer for buildings.
When the settlers had gone, the area around Suffield became the "New Mexico" of Canada. It was used by Canada, Britain and the United States as a supersecret testing ground, chiefly for poison gas, but also for explosives and other weapons. The area is now a permanent military experimental station, including three camps and an airfield, that cost more than $8 millions.
The 130 families scattered across Canada and the United States. Some of them refused to accept a cent of the award. All of them felt that they had been treated unfairly, that the people of the "British block" got less than British justice. Now they want the question reopened. The united farmers of Alberta support their appeal for arbitration.
After that article appeared in this magazine, one of the members of the board who had something to do with making settlement with these farmers put another article in Maclean's magazine. I read that article, as I have no doubt many other hon. members did, and after reading it I wrote to the Minister of National Defence suggesting that the case be reopened and further consideration be given the farmers. I thought that possibly that would be done, but this, in part, is the letter which I received from the minister dated April 30, 1947:
A short time ago Maclean's magazine published an article on this matter with the result that one of the men who acted for this department wrote a letter to Mr. Horace T. Hunter, president of the Maclean-Hunter publishing Company Limited, copy of which is enclosed, and which I think deals with the matter thoroughly.
That is the letter I got in reply to my letter to the minister. I will read the letter to Mr. Hunter. It is quite a long letter, but I will read it and another letter before I am through. It is dated March 14, 1947, and is addressed to Mr. Horace T. Hunter, president
Supply-National Defence

Maclean-Hunter Publishing Company Limited, 481 University avenue, Toronto 2, Ontario. It reads:
Dear Sir:	An item "Cross Country-The
Prairies," which appears on page 72 of the March 15, 1947, issue of Maclean's magazine, is the type of misleading malicious report which is fuel for communist propaganda.
May I digress for a moment. First of all, I want to say that the man who wrote this letter did not know the first thing of what he was talking about. If he had lived in that area, as many of the farmers, and as I myself have done, he certainly would not say that it was communist propaganda.
But he did not say that in the letter. He said that the article was fuel for communist propaganda.
That is exactly what he said, and he certainly did not know the facts or he would not have said that. I know every farmer who resided in that area and I am sure there was not a communist there.
But he does not say that. He does not say there was a communist there. He says that that kind of attitude, that kind of misstatement, would be fuel for communist propaganda.

I will accept the statement of the minister, but I still contend that he should have kept that out of this letter. He goes on:
As a member of the real estate adviser's staff who proceeded to Medicine Hat in May, 1944, to acquire the "British block," comprising approximately 1,100 square miles, and which was so urgently needed at that time by the British government for experimental purposes, I am fully aware of all the facts, which are as follows:
I do not know the details of any offers which might have been made to the owners of the property prior to May, 1941, before the real estate adviser's branch was requested to take over, but I know no progress had been made in obtaining this land.
Lieut.-Col. Goodwin Gibson, O.B.E., at that time real estate adviser to the Department of National Defence, and presently president of Gibson Brothers, Toronto, assembled at Medicine Hat the following:
Mr. H. A. Dyde, O.B.E., lawyer, Department of National Defence, presently practising law in Edmonton; Mr. G. M. Bowes, O.B.E., of the real estate adviser's office, Department of National Defence, presently vice-president, Oldfield, Kirby and Gardner, Winnipeg; Mr. Frank W. Collins, industrial commissioner, Canadian Pacific Railway; Mr. G. H. S. Dinsmore, assistant to real estate adviser, Department of National Defence, presently director, lands and buildings, War _ Assets Corporation; Mr. J. Wurtele Rankin, O.B.E., assistant to real estate adviser, Department of National Defence, presently vicepresident, Westmount Realties Company, Montreal; Mr. Harry Allum, chief field representative, soldiers' settlement board for Western Canada, Edmonton, presently head of Depart-

ment of Veterans Affairs, Edmonton, Alta; fifteen field representatives of the soldiers' settlement board from all sections of Western Canada; Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel stenographers, et cetera.
Because of the urgency of possession, the property was expropriated, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were used to distribute the notices of expropriation over this huge area, and they had nothing whatever to do with issuing summonses to farmers to appear in court in Medicine Hat. The expropriation w'as dated June 4, 1941, and everyone had to be off the area by July 1.
The court house in Medicine Hat was loaned to the real estate adviser's department only because there was no other suitable vacant space available in Medicine Hat, and it was just coincidental that this location was obtained.
Digressing for a moment from the letter, may I say that according to the letter the court house was used entirely for this purpose. At that time my office was in the court house and they certainly did not use my office. It is quite true they used a small space in there, but once again this writer is wrong. I continue :
A complete inventory and valuation of each owner's property was made by field representatives of the soldiers' settlement .board, who are acknowledged as being well versed in prairie farm values, and who worked day and night to accomplish the task in short order.
The buildings were put in at full value to the farm, and not the depreciated value as they should have been. After paying the owners for the buildings, they (the owners) were given the right to remove any or all buildings, fences or equipment, and as a result many buildings were moved to Medicine Hat and elsewhere, and are in use today.
Among allowances given were $3 per head for driving off cattle, $4 for each horse, 50 cents for each sheep, being amounts determined by drovers and cattlemen as being fair and reasonable; $3 per ton in stacks for -what went as hay but -which would not be regarded in better areas as feed at all; from $50 to $250', depending on the size of the family and the distance from Medicine Hat, was allowed for moving expenses, 25 cents per foot for each dug well, 5 cents per acre per year, limited to ten years, for unexpired ranch leases, the rentals of which -were in many cases in default and yearly grazing leases had not been renewed but were recognized just the same.
In regard to the type of land, the biggest rancher in the area had about 40.000 acres under lease and, by drilling gas wells by the river, obtained power to pump water by which he irrigated some three thousand acres of land. In this way, he was able to grow alfalfa grass and thus obtain winter feed for his herds. In spite of this, however, his foreman claimed that the land could only support thirty head on each section of 640 acres. This should show that $4 per acre was a generous amount for raw land of this description, but it should be noted that as high as I think, $27 per acre was paid for some of the best land. Naturally, in such a large area, the type of land varied and was priced accordingly.
In spite, however, of all the allowances given to the various owners, it was found in many

Betrothal oj Princess. Elizabeth
cases that their accumulated debts were still greater than what could be allowed them. Colonel Gibson contacted Hon. Mr. W. A. Fallow, at that time Minister of Agriculture of the province of Alberta-
May I digress just here for a moment and say that Mr. Fallow was never minister of agriculture of Alberta. Mr. Fallow is minister of public works of Alberta. The minister of agriculture of Alberta at that time was Mr. D.	B. Mullen, if I am not mistaken. To continue:
-and appealed for help for these unfortunates. As a result, the province generously agreed to forgive all debts up to the point where $d>500 could be paid these settlers for their lands and buildings with the other allowances made added to that amount.
The owners of the cultivated land had the opportunity of either accepting $4 per acre for standing crops, or could harvest their crops, whichever they chose, blit could not live on the land after July 1, 194.1. Practically all decided to accept the $4 per acre for crops, and as for the very few who did not, I understand they did not net more than the amount offered for standing crops. This area is in a dry belt, occupation of the area should never have been permitted in the first place, and it was a godsend to get these settlers off this type of land.
Six o'clock.
May we call it six o'clock.

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OF INCOME AND OTHER TAXES

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Abbott for the second reading of Bill No. 411, to authorize the government to enter into agreement with the governments of the provinces pursuant to which, in return for compensation, the provinces agree to refrain from levying certain taxes for a limited period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OF INCOME AND OTHER TAXES
speechtext:
The bill now before the house embodies the final outcome of negotiations that



Tax Agreements with Provinces
have extended over a period of almost two years. It authorizes the governor in council to enter into agreements with provincial governments embodying the terms and conditions so negotiated, it gives authority to carry out certain ancillary actions, ajid it provides the necessary appropriations.
As hon. members well know, the arrangements which have been agreed upon represent a compromise with our original objectives which we found it impossible to achieve, because of the failure to reach agreement with all of the nine provinces. I do not intend by that statement to cast blame in any direction. I am only stating a fact. I cannot let the occasion pass, however, without again affirming that the dominion government has made every effort to reach unanimous agreement, and far from being rigid and uncompromising in its attitude, as has been alleged on several occasions during the course of the negotiations, it has repeatedly made adjustments in its proposals, repeatedly accepted suggestions put forward by various provincial governments, repeatedly made concessions to secure unanimous agreement. In order, therefore, to place the present position in its proper perspective, I wish to say a word about its historical background and then to review briefly and simply the course of the protracted negotiations from 1945 to date.
The genesis of the current phase of dominion-provincial relations dates back to the financial difficulties faced by several provinces during the depression years of the thirties. In spite of large dominion grants in aid and heavy construction expenditure, the burden of unemployment relief had been such as to weaken the financial position of all provincial governments, but in the prairie west drought and depressed agricultural prices had created an additional, almost intolerable strain, leading to default on the part of Alberta and threatening the solvency of the other two provinces. Further financial assistance of an interim character was granted to Manitoba and Saskatchewan as a result of reports made by the Bank of Canada in the spring of 1937 but it had already become clear that no permanent or satisfactory solution could be developed without a fundamental inquiry into the financial powers and responsibilities of Canadian governing bodies at all levels. This led to the establishment in August 1937 of a royal commission, first under the chairmanship of the Honourable Justice N. W. Rowell of Toronto, later under that of Doctor Joseph Sirois of Quebec, to inquire into the constitutional allo-

cation of revenue sources and governmental burdens in Canada and-
. . . to express what in their opinion, subject to the retention of the distribution of legislative powers essential to the proper carrying out of the federal system in harmony with national needs and the promotion of national unity, will best effect a balanced relationship between the financial powers and the obligations and functions of each governing body and conduce to a more efficient, independent and economical discharge of governmental responsibilities in Canada.
If I may say so, that statement, extracted from order in council P.C. 1908 of August 14, 1937, of the high objective of a healthy and vigorous federal system of government, has remained throughout the long years and the changing circumstances since that time the fundamental objective of the government of Canada.
After the most thorough-going and comprehensive inquiry into the problems of federal government ever undertaken in the history of any state, the commission submitted its report on May 3, 1940, nearly three years later and after the outbreak of war. Stated very briefly, its chief recommendations were: (1) exclusive dominion jurisdiction in the fields of income and corporation taxes and succession duties;
(2)	acceptance by the dominion of responsibility for relief to the employable unemployed;
(3)	assumption by the dominion of net provincial debt charges; and (4) payment by the dominion of national adjustment grants designed to put each provincial government in a position to provide average standards of services without imposing higher than average rates of taxation.
A dominion-provincial conference was called in January 1941, to consider the royal commission's report but after sitting two or three days the conference broke down in the face of opposition from the premiers of three provinces.
It soon became apparent, however, that Canada's chaotic tax structure would not permit the financing on either an efficient or an equitable basis of a war effort of the magnitude which the necessities of the second world war were to make imperative. Consequently, in the budget of April 29, 1941, the then minister of finance made an offer to the effect that if the provincial governments (and their municipalities) were prepared to suspend imposition of income and corporation taxes until the end of the war and one year thereafter the dominion government would make annual payments to the provinces equal to either the 1940 revenues of the particular province from these sources or the amount of that province's net debt service less succession duty

Tax Agreements loith Provinces
collections in 1940. The offer also included some relatively small "fiscal need" subsidies proposed in those cases where budgets could not otherwise be balanced, and an offer to guarantee provincial gasoline tax revenues at the 1940 level. Agreements were negotiated with all the provincial governments in 1941 and the necessary legislation was passed in the spring of 1942. I think it not unfair to say that it is impossible to exaggerate the contribution which this co-operative arrangement made to the efficient and equitable financing of the war, to the maintenance of Canada's financial stability during the war, and consequently to Canada's ability to meet the financial and economic problems of postwar reconstruction.
It was our experience with these war-time tax agreements and the knowledge that after their termination a number of the pre-war financial and constitutional problems would probably arise in an exaggerated form that led the dominion government to take the initiative in preparing the way for postwar agreements with the provinces. After a great deal of consideration over a period of many months, there had been worked out a comprehensive set of proposals which were broader in scope than the Sirois report recommendations but were framed in an earnest effort to avoid, if at all possible, the major objections that had caused the rejection of those recommendations. The agreement was to be for a temporary period and therefore its terms would be subject to review prior to any renewal. In particular it would require no constitutional changes, although there was one recommendation for a constitutional amendment to provide for delegation of powers from the dominion government to a provincial government or vice versa, whenever desired by both governments. Other less important features were designed to avoid possible objections.
The purpose of the dominion in preparing these proposals was to endeavour to work out with the provinces a coordinated programme by which the dominion and provincial governments could most effectively work together to maintain high and expanding levels of employment and national income such as had been attained in war time, to provide a wide measure of economic and social security, and finally to give the Canadian people a less burdensome, more efficient tax system, which indeed was a prerequisite for attaining the other objectives. In the field of public welfare, the proposals included constructive measures for a programme of health insurance and health grants, a comprehensive scheme of pensions for the aged and the blind and the provision of unemployment assistance, with the whole or a substantial share of the cost 83166-339J
being borne by the dominion. In the field of public investment the dominion outlined a substantial expansion in its programme for natural resource development, conservation and public works, and also a large increase in dominion assistance to provincial services and construction projects either through joint participation oir by grants in aid. Particular emphasis was placed upon, and tangible encouragement offered to, the advance planning of public projects, and in so far as practicable, the timing of public investment expenditures with a view to helping stabilize employment and offset fluctuations in the business cycle.
To avoid duplication and conflict in the tax field and to enable ithe dominion to develop an equitable and efficient tax system, the proposals included a provision that the provincial governments should rent to the dominion for the term of the agreement their rights in the fields of income and corporation taxes and succession duties. As compensation or rental therefor, the dominion would make annual payments to the provinces on the basis of $12 per capita of provincial population, with an adjustment for increases in gross national product per capita over the base year 1941. These payments would include the ordinary statutory subsidies. This formula would guarantee the provinces a minimum annual payment of $138 million and for a year in which the national income had risen to $950 per capita, as is now roughly estimated for 1947, the formula would call for a total payment of about $195 million. The dominion felt at the time that payments of this magnitude, coupled with the various other proposals in the field of public investment and social security, would enable all provincial governments to carry out their constitutional responsibilities with assurance and adequacy; under prosperous conditions they would be expected to have surpluses, perhaps even substantial surpluses, but at the same time they would be projected against any major deterioration in revenues when business fell below normal. If I may quote from the so-called Green Book proposals (page 51):
To sum up, it is the belief of the dominion government that the proposed financial arrangements in conjunction with the other measures recommended would strengthen the federal system under which all ten governments here represented function. They would give to each government an assured basis of financial responsibility and freedom of decision in the matters entrusted to it by the constitution.
The proposals of the dominion were presented to the provinces in a dominion-provin-
Tax Agreements with Provinces

cial conference held in Ottawa during the week beginning August 6, 1945-incidentally, the week which saw the surrender of Japan and the end of world war II.
At this conference, the provincial governments accepted the dominion's proposals as a basis for discussion. It was suggested, however, that better progress could be made if an opportunity were given to all governments for studying the proposals and if the procedure was such as to avoid projecting controversial issues into public discussion. It was therefore decided to establish a coordinating committee, composed of the heads of the various governments, to consider further procedure and to examine in detail the proposals made by the dominion as well as those that might be made by any other government.
This coordinating committee met in November, 1945, in camera and there was a full and frank discussion of the important issues involved. At this meeting it was decided to establish an economic committee composed of technical representatives of the dominion and nine provincial governments to examine in detail all the dominion's proposals against the background of the economic prospects that might be expected during the period of the agreement. This committee carried on its work during the months of December, 1945, and January, 1946, giving detailed consideration not only to the dominion's financial, social security and public investment proposals but also to proposals made by certain of the provinces, particularly those of the province of Ontario.
In January, 1946, the coordinating committee was reconvened to discuss the dominion's proposals and any alternatives advanced by provincial governments in the light of the findings of the economic committee. This conference, which lasted for several days, was also held in camera but there was later public disclosure of the fact that the dominion had made substantial concessions to the provinces, in particular the proposal to increase the guaranteed minimum payment from 812 to S15 per capita with adjustments from the 1942 base for increases in provincial population and in gross national product per capita. Two additional options were provided. In the first place, no province was to receive less than 82 million, an option designed to fit the special case of Prince Edward Island, and in the second place, any province had the right to accept as its minimum 150 per cent of the amount which it had been receiving from the dominion under its war-time tax agreement, an option which had special appeal for British Columbia. The effect of these

proposals was to increase the total of the guaranteed minimum payments to the provinces from 8138 million to 8180-4 million, an increase of over thirty per cent. The dominion also gave an undertaking in this conference that it would not enter certain fields of taxation which the provinces were currently cultivating, would not increase certain of its own excise taxes, and would undertake to seek a new constitutional amendment that would allow the provinces to impose a limited retail sales tax. Certain modifications were also proposed in the public welfare measures, which entailed additional commitments by the dominion.
Like its two predecessors, the January conference adjourned without reaching a decision but it was decided to hold a further meeting at the end of April, 1946. During a two-day session in camera, the dominion answered certain questions that had been asked by provincial premiers, and made an important modification of its earlier proposals, the effect of which was to allow any province to remain in the succession duty field if it so wished, in which case an appropriate adjustment would be made in the annual payment due to it. It was then decided to move the conference into plenary session and public meetings were held daily from April 29 to May 3. In these open sessions the dominion proposals as revised from time to time in the preceding conferences were presented and discussed. An alternative proposal was presented by the premier of Ontario which was found unacceptable to this government because of the large additional cost which we estimated it would involve to the dominion treasury. In its revised proposals the dominion felt that it had made as comprehensive an offer and had undertaken to assume as great a financial burden as it then believed it possible to justify to the people of Canada. The negotiations had already extended over nine months and during that period of time the dominion had repeatedly revised its proposals in the endeavour to meet the several requests made by the provinces. The dominion was still willing to accept suggestions for modification of its proposals provided that they did not further increase the burden upon the taxpayers of Canada. In particular and because of the strongly expressed desire of several provinces to have fields of taxation solely for their own use, the then minister of finance expressed the dominion's willingness to rent for a temporary period our rights to use certain fields of excise tax (gasoline taxes, amusement taxes, taxes on pari-mutuel bets) in the same way as we were asking the provinces to rent to us temporarily their rights in certain fields of direct

Tax Agreements with Provinces
taxation. However, there was no agreement reached among the provinces with respect to an appropriate rental consideration. On May 3 the conference adjourned sine die without any agreement having been reached.
Failure of these protracted efforts to achieve general agreement on its comprehensive proposals posed a difficult problem for the dominion, as well of course as for at least several of the provincial governments. The dominion budget had to be brought down within a matter of weeks. The war-time tax agreements were to lapse in the case of three provinces in the late fall and in the case of all other provinces in the spring of 1947. Under these wartime agreements, the dominion was committed to making certain reductions, in its income and corporation taxes as from January 1, 1947, but it could not simply carry out its commitments and remain indifferent to the financial problems which at least the less favoured provinces were bound to face. For several of these provinces the pre-war situation had been intolerable but meanwhile provincial expenditures had expanded greatly and while revenues had also increased to some extent, it was obvious that without new agreements several provinces were going to be faced with a difficult budget problem. Financial pressure on these provinces, it was clear, would give rise to increasingly arbitrary and discriminatory taxation tending to hamper production, would lead to interference with interprovincial trade, and would tend to promote the extension of government operation of business merely in order to obtain additional provincial revenues, which of course would mean loss of revenues to the dominion. An inefficient and chaotic tax structure might seriously impair the capacity of private enterprise to provide high and expanding employment. Budget difficulties and financial pressures would tend to weaken the financial autonomy of the provinces and impair the strength of the federal system. Some provinces might indeed find it difficult to maintain their solvency.
After very careful consideration the government reached the conclusion that it would be shirking its responsibility to the people of Canada if it allowed such a situation to develop without a further attempt to prevent it. It sought therefore to devise some modified proposal which could be accepted by those provinces which wished to accept it and be left aside by those which did not desire it or felt they had no need for it. It was this type of proposal which the then minister of finance outlined in his budget speech of June 27, 1946. Without the prospect of unanimous agreement, it was necessary to limit
the proposal to the financial provisions relating to the rental of tax fields. No changes were suggested in the formula for calculating the annual payments to the provinces but the proposal as a whole was so designed that any province that did not accept its terms could impose its own taxes without placing its taxpayers in an unfair position relative to the taxpayers in other provinces. The agreeing provinces, for example, were to impose a 5 per cent tax on the income of their corporations, so that a corporation in a non-agreeing province which imposed a tax no higher than that rate would be in the same position as a corporation in an agreeing province. The dominion also offered to allow a taxpayer a credit against his personal income tax up to five per cent for personal income taxes paid to a province; this would allow a non-agreeing province to impose a tax of this weight *without subjecting its citizens to double taxation. Finally, the dominion proposed that its succession duty rates should be doubled and a credit given up to one-half thereof for duties paid to a provincial government, as a means of allowing any government, including that of an agreeing province, to continue to impose succession duties if it so wished.
As I have siacedl, the formula for calculating the annual payments to the provinces was the same as that outlined to the dominion-provincial conference by the Prime Minister on April 29, 1946. However, in the course of the negotiations with individual provinces during the months following the delivery of the budget, the government became convinced that these financial terms, standing alone and extracted from the broader context of the original proposals which provided assistance in other forms to the provincial governments, might prove inadequate in certain cases to protect a province against the rising costs of government that might be anticipated in the years ahead. This was particularly true of the special formulae, applicable to the provinces of Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, as the flat payment of $2 million in the one case, and the payment based on 150 per cent of the war-time tax agreement receipts in the other case, were not subject to adjustment for increases in population and gross national product. To correct this situation, the dominion first undertook that these minimum payments to Prince Edward Island and British Columbia would be subject to adjustment for increases in population and gross national product. Later, when it was urged by the other provinces that the basis of their compensation should also be reviewed, a modification of the original formula was worked out, and made applicable
Tax Agreements with Provinces

to all provinces, in January 1947, under which it is believed the maximum practicable degree of "equalization" of the terms of payment to the various provinces has been achieved.
Under the new formula every province will have a guaranteed minimum annual payment which will be subject to adjustment upward for increases in provincial population and in gross national product per capita, in just the same way as for all other provinces. For the province of Prince Edward Island, the guaranteed minimum will be the flat sum of $2,100,000. All other provinces will have the choice of either one of two formulae for determining their guaranteed minimum annual payment.
As the house will recall, the first option involves the addition of the three following elements:
1.	$12.75 per capita based on the 1942 population of the province;
2.	Fifty per cent of the revenue of the province from income and corporation taxes for the year ending nearest to December 31, 1940, as agreed for purposes of the wartime tax agreement; and
3.	the amount of the statutory subsidies payable to the province in 1947.
This option is the one which proves to be most favourable in the case of New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia. It will be noted that it has the great merit of including in the guaranteed minimum payments the amounts of the statutory subsidies payable to the various provinces, which have been the product of eighty years of historical development and negotiation. For the rest this particular option is based on a reasonable compromise between the principle of basing the annual grants on equal per capita payments and the principle of adjusting the grants to the varying capacity of the provinces to raise revenues from the tax sources which they are renting to the dominion. The greatest weight is placed on the principle of equality but at the same time reasonable weight is given to the principle of tax ability or tax potential, which is of advantage to the more favoured provinces, and reasonable weight also to the principle of need, which is reflected in the statutory subsidies and which is of course of greatest advantage to the less favoured provinces.
The second option gives the province the right to receive a guaranteed minimum annual payment equal to the sum of its statutory subsidies payable in 1947 and an amount equal to $15 per capita based on the 1942 population of the province. This is the option which
rMr. Abbott.]
proves most favourable to the provinces of Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan. In the case of Nova Scotia the province had not been cultivating the fields of income and corporation taxes as intensively as other provinces in the base year of the war-time tax agreement and in the case of Saskatchewan prevailing economic conditions in that province had led to a relatively low yield from* these tax fields in 1940. It could have been contended, therefore, that the first option would not be fair to either of these two provinces, and consequently the second option was worked out to meet their special situations.
With the consent of the house I shall now place on Hansard a table showing the calculation of the guaranteed minimum annual payment for each province, as well as a table showing how the adjusted annual payments for 1947 are calculated and how they work out for each province on the basis of the latest data now available.
