The amount payable by Canada to any province in respect of any fiscal year is to be estimated forthwith after September 14 in the said year on the basis of certificates from the dominion statistician in regard to the gross national production ratios and the provincial ratios that are pertinent to the calculation. The excess of this amount over the ordinary statutory subsidies less certain deductions which I shall later describe, is to be paid to the province in four equal quarterly instalments on September 30, December 31, March 31 and June 30, respectively. Appropriate provision is made for adjustments in respect of recalculations made after September 15, in the following fiscal year on the basis of revised estimates of population and gross national product. A final adjustment is also to be made at the termination of the agreement in 1952. At that time the population figures obtained by the census for the year 1951 will be available and it will thus be possible to correct earlier estimates of population made by the dominion statistician on the basis of a straight line projection between the base year 1942, or, in the case of the prairie provinces, the census year 1946, on the one hand, and the census year 1951 on the other hand. If changes or improvements in the method of calculating the gross national product have been made by the dominion statistician during the course of the agreement which result in a series of amounts for the gross national product different from those produced by the method used at the beginning of the agreement, the province will be given the benefit
in the final calculation at the end of the agreement of whichever method results in the greater total of payments for the period of the agreement.
I referred a few minutes ago to certain deductions which are required to be made from the amounts otherwise payable to the provinces.
The first of these types of deduction arises from the rather complicated provisions which have had to be evolved in order to avoid substantial unfairness as between the corporate taxpayers of agreeing and non-agreeing provinces respectively. If a province chooses to remain out of the agreement, it will presumably have to levy taxes on its own corporations in order to secure adequate revenues, and there would therefore be unfairness if the government of an agreeing province were to receive full payment from the dominion for the rental of its corporate tax rights while at the same time its corporations were not subject to provincial tax. Consequently, even though an essential part of the new agreements involves the dominion renting full provincial rights in the corporate tax field, nevertheless the agreements contain clauses allowing adhering provinces to impose a standard of five per cent tax on corporate income earned within the province, to be collected by the dominion without cost to the province, and providing that the amounts otherwise payable to a province shall be reduced by either the amount of the provincial corporation tax actually collected or one-sixth of the dominion corporate tax relevant to corporate incomes earned within the particular province, whichever is the greater. It will be noted that no province is required to levy this tax but if a province chooses not to levy it, the payments it will receive from the dominion are correspondingly reduced. Incidentally, the agreement includes carefully worked out provisions for allocating as between the various provinces the income of a corporation which is operating in more than one province; it is believed that if these rules for allocating income were adopted by all provinces, there would be eliminated the tendency which prevailed at times in the past for various provincial governments to impose tax, in the aggregate, on more than the total income of a corporation carrying on business in several provinces. The agreements also contain a provision to the effect that if Canada so requests, all the agreeing provinces will take such steps as are necessary to repeal or suspend their legislation imposing the standard five per cent tax on corporate income.
Tax Agreements with Provinces

The second type of deduction from the annual amounts otherwise payable to an agreeing province, relates to deductions which may be made if a province which has agreed to rent its corporation taxes to the dominion proceeds to take over the whole or any part of the business or undertaking or assets of a corporation and thus serves to reduce the tax revenues which the dominion would otherwise obtain. This section of the agreement has been worked out with great care but I need not go into all its complications.
I should at this point call special attention to a provision of the bill which is of an entirety different character. Stated briefly, this provision authorizes the dominion to pay to a provincial government one-half of its net collections of tax on the income of certain specified public utility corporations resulting from the distribution to the public or the generation for distribution to the public, of electricity, gas or steam in the province concerned. From these payments is to be deducted the amount of certain royalties or rentals and taxes and fees paid by the corporations concerned to the government of the said province or its municipalities. This refund of part of the dominion's collections of taxes from specified public utility corporations will apply not only to governments which have entered into agreements with the dominion but also to the governments of non-adhering provinces as well. The only difference between an adhering and a non-adhering province in this respect will be that in the former case the dominion will be bound to make these refunds for the five-year term of the agreement. In the other case, it will have the power to do so but will not be bound.
There is another provision of the bill to which I should call attention. In addition to making provision for the guaranteed minimum annual payments and the adjusted annual payments for all agreeing provinces for the five fiscal years beginning April 1, 1947, there is a provision in the bill which authorizes special payments to be made to the maritime provinces to fill in the so-called gap in their case between the beginning of the new agreements, April 1, 1947, and the end of the old wartime tax agreements-October 31, 1946, in the case of New Brunswick, November 30, 1946. in the case of Nova Scotia, and December 31, 1946, in the case of Prince Edward Island. These payments are the appropriate fraction in each case of the guaranteed minimum annual payments to each province less the proportionate amount of the statutory subsidies payable in respect of the periods in
[Mr. Abbott. 1
question and less deductions in respect of provincial succession duties collected by the province or allowed by the dominion as credits in respect of deaths during these periods. Before the deduction relating to succession duties, the amount is 82,975,430 for New Brunswick, $360,768 for Prince Edward Island and 82,955,000 for Nova Scotia. These payments are 'to be charged as an expenditure to the fiscal year 1946-47.
There is only one other provision of the bill or the agreement to which I feel I should call attention at this time and that is the option provided to adhering provinces in the ease of succession duties. Any province may come into the agreement and still retain its own succession duty levies if it wishes to do so. The dominion believes that there are important reasons to justify the elimination of double taxation in this field but at the same time it recognizes that certain provincial governments place special emphasis on the desirability of continuing to levy their own succession duties. In the desire to remove any obstacle that might otherwise prove an insuperable barrier to unanimous agreement, the dominion has made it possible for any province -which so desires to rent to the dominion only its rights in the field of income and corporation taxes and to retain its own succession duty levies. In such a case, taxpayers in the said province will receive a credit against the dominion succession duty of the amount of the duty paid to the province up to one-half of the dominion levy and the annual payments otherwise payable to the province by the dominion will be reduced by the aggregate of such tax credits.
Before I conclude, I wish to deal briefly with a few general aspects of these agreements.
My first point has to do with the basis of determining the amount of rental we are to pay for the tax fields in question. Our contention is that our formulae represent the most equitable and most realistic basis so far devised for determining the rentals to be paid to the various provinces. I have been asked why we have not based them solely on the principle of equal per capita grants. The simple answer to that question is that it would be inequitable. Equal per capita grants may sound like equality but, if so, the equality is of a very specious type. It is certainty not equity.
For one thing, you cannot consider separ-atety each type of assistance given by the dominion in the various provinces. If you put these on a per capita basis and look at each one alone, you get the most amazing results. Take the statutory subsidies, for

Tax Agreements with. Provinces
instance. Based on 1946 population estimates, they run all the way from about 80 cents per capita in the two central provinces to $1 in British Columbia, 82.36 in Manitoba, $2.45 in Saskatchewan, $2.51 in Alberta, $3.28 in Nova Scotia, $3.40 in New Brunswick, and $6.99 in Prince Edward Island. Yet in spite of these wide variations, no one would regard the subsidies as unfair-on the contrary, the variations represent the historical result of a series of attempts to achieve equitable treatment under very diverse conditions. Then, as another instance, take the family allowance payments. Here it is British Columbia which turns out to have the lowest per capita payment ($16.11 for the twelve months ended May 31, 1947), while Quebec has one of the highest per capita payments ($23.04), against an average of $20.26 for the country as a whole. No one could regard these variations as unfair, nor the similar variations in the dominion's per capita contributions to pensions for aged and blind persons. However, if we take all these payments by the dominion, including the animal rental payments to be made for the rented taxes under our latest offer, we will find that the aggregate per capita payments to the various provinces are very much closer to equality. On this basis the average for Canada as a whole is $42.54, with S41.29 for British Columbia, and S43.83 for Quebec.
But even this greater approach to equality on a per capita basis should not be overstressed because-and this is my second point -equality per unit or per head does not represent equity, if the units or the heads differ in character or importance. The fact is that the units do differ-and differ widely- because of the varying composition of the population in the various provinces. In other words, the percentage of children in the population, the size of families, the relative numbers of adult income earners and of taxpayers -all these factors and others vary from province to province. It should be obvious that this type of variation makes it quite impossible to satisfy the test of equity by making annual payments to the provinces on the basis of an equal amount per head of population.
There are some who realize that equal per capita payments would be unfair but ask why our annual payments should not be based on the principle of fiscal need. It should be clear from the figures I gave some time ago that our basis for determining the annual payments does recognize this principle of fiscal need to a very substantial extent. The reason that certain provinces may be in a
position of fiscal need (assuming that it has not been due to reckless spending in the past) is that the head offices of large corporations as well as the wealthy individuals and large estates are concentrated to a very substantial extent in two or three provinces, and consequently it is impossible for the other provinces to derive from income and corporation taxes and succession duties adequate revenues to meet their constitutional responsibilities. Now the proposals which we are making are designed to correct this difficulty. What they accomplish is to make sure that a maritime province or a prairie province is able, by renting its rights in the three great fields of direct progressive taxation to the dominion, to derive approximately as much revenue per capita from these major sources of revenue as any other province.
I contend therefore that the proposals meet substantially the test of fiscal need but they do it in a way which is not open to the objections to which ordinary fiscal need grants are subject. If we adopted in toto the principle of grants on the basis of fiscal need, I suggest to hon. members that we would be faced with this . dilemma:	Either the government of
Canada would be forced to raise money from the taxpayers of Canada as a whole and hand it over to provincial governments to meet their deficits, no matter how reckless their expenditure policy might be, or, conversely, the dominion would be forced to supervise the budgetary policies, including both the spending and the tax levying policies, of provincial governments. This government does not believe the first policy would commend itself to Canadian taxpayers and it will resist to the utmost any proposal which would require it to supervise the budgets of provincial governments.
We are forced to the conclusion, therefore, that there is no single principle which can be applied exclusively in determining the magnitude of these annual rental payments. Our formulae are based on the several principles which seem to be pertinent. They may seem complicated but, we believe, the complications are necessary if we are to meet fairly and equitably the varying needs and conditions of all the provinces.
My second point relates to a problem which led to a good deal of discussion during the negotiations, namely, the treatment of cert-tain minor fields of taxation. It was understandable that the provinces generally would desire to have, if possible, certain tax fields specifically reserved for their own use. The levies which they most frequently requested should be left to them exclusively were sue-
Tax Agreements with Provinces

cession duties and taxes on gasoline, amusements, pari-mutuel bets and electricity.
In appraising this request, it is desirable to call attention to four or five relevant considerations.
First, to grant the request would not be in accord with the constitution, for the British North America Act quite clearly provides that the dominion government has full authority to impose taxation by any mode or method whatsoever, whereas the provincial governments are limited to direct taxation.
In the second place it is always desirable to remember that in the case of war or emergency it is the central government upon which responsibility must fall. It was probably for this reason that the fathers of confederation felt that the dominion's taxing powers should be unrestricted and their wise foresight has now been amply confirmed by Canada's experience in two world wars.
Thirdly, it had to be remembered that any sacrifice of these minor taxes by the dominion would almost certainly under prevailing conditions of revenue and expenditure and with the national debt at so high a figure have to be made up by increases in income tax, a tax already at such high rates and so steeply graduated, that in the minds of most people it constituted or was likely to constitute a serious impediment to increased employment, production and national income.
In the fourth place, some of the taxes over which the provinces sought exclusive jurisdiction would bring important advantages, if collected solely by the dominion. I refer particularly to succession duties. I shall not repeat here the various arguments advanced by the Sirois commission and others for transferring or renting this tax field to the dominion but I believe most people would agree that the pre-war system under which nine separate jurisdictions impose succession duties, resulting in double and sometimes triple taxation of the same estate, producing great variations in burden as between one province and another and tending to encourage transfer of estates from one province to another solely for tax reasons, was burdensome, inequitable and harmful to the free flow of capital and natural economic development. Perhaps an even more compelling reason from the dominion's point of view is the very important part which dominion succession duties play in contributing to an efficient enforcement of the income tax. The former deputy minister of national revenue (taxation) has stated that we get more revenue from them indirectly than we do directly. However, in spite of the powerful
(Mr. Abbott.]
arguments for unified collection by the dominion of succession duties we recognized, as I have already said the apparent strength of the desire of one or two provinces to remain in this field and we modified our offer in such a way that any province which wished to do so could continue levying its own succession duties. I am happy to be able to report that all of the seven provinces which have signified their intention of entering into agreements with us apparently expect to repeal their succession duties for the term of the agreement.
Finally, neither the government of Canada, nor anyone else, so far as I am aware has ever been able to discover any way in which the total tax field could be divided' between the dominion and provincial governments in such a way as to make it possible for the dominion government on the one hand and all provincial governments on the other hand to obtain from the sector of the field allotted to each the revenues required to carry out their constitutional responsibilities. It would of course be possible to assign such a portion . of the tax field exclusively to provincial governments as to enable some provincial governments to meet their requirements but most methods of allocation would leave other provinces in a weak or impossible position financially. This of course arises from the highly different potential yields of different taxes in various provinces, and is one of the major factors making it so difficult to get all provinces to agree on any single course of action in the fiscal field. To approach the objective of meeting the requirements of the less favoured provinces as well as of those most, favoured1 would mean assigning to provincial governments so large a portion of the total field as to make it completely impossible for the dominion to meet its responsibilities.
In spite of all these considerations, the dominion has gone very far in its endeavour to meet, the wishes of provincial governments in this connection. In the revised offer outlined by the right hon. the Prime Minister to the dominion-provincial conference in April-May, 1946, the dominion made several commitments in regard to its future tax policy, lit undertook for the duration of the agreement not to enter the fields of real estate tax and automobile licenses now exclusively occupied by the provinces. It agreed to allow the provinces to tax mining and logging operations either by royalties or by taxes on the net profit of these operations, and to recognize such levies as an expense for purposes of dominion tax. It undertook for the duration of the agreement not to increase its

Tax Agreements with Provinces
special excise taxes on gasoline, amusements or pari-mutuel betting, subject of course to the condition that in the event of a national emergency it would be free to take whatever steps might he necessary to meet the emergency. It undertook to pay to the provinces one half of its own net collections of tax on the income of certain specified public utility companies derived from the distribution to the public, or the generating for distribution to the public, of electrical energy, gas or steam. It undertook to seek a constitutional amendment permitting delegation of powers from the dominion parliament to provincial legislatures or vice versa, and it stated that once such an amendment was made the dominion government would request parliament to broaden considerably the field of provincial taxation by delegating to the provinces, for the duration of the agreement, the right to levy retail sales taxes within limits to be specifically defined. Finally, it stated that, while in view of the enormous financial burdens and responsibilities falling upon the central government, it could not in justice to the taxpayers of Canada increase the magnitude of the burdens which as a result of the new proposals it was undertaking to bear, nevertheless it would be willing to consider renting to the provinces for an appropriate financial equivalent agreed upon by the provinces the field) of gasoline tax and some of the other minor tax fields. This meant that the dominion was offering to rent to the provinces its own rights in certain specified fields of taxation for an agreed consideration, just as it was offering to rent from the provinces their rights in certain other fields of taxation for a consideration which all will agree is highly advantageous to the provinces.
Several of the provinces expressed themselves as willing to accept this offer but they were unable to agree on an appropriate rental for the reason mentioned above, what one province would accept as a fair rental was believed to be highly unfair or inappropriate by another province. Nevertheless the dominion continued to give careful study to this whole problem. Late last fall, the prospect of substantial improvement in dominion revenues made it possible to sacrifice $40,000,000 of expected revenue by dropping as from April 1 this year, its three cent a gallon tax on gasoline. Not only was this tax the most important of the minor taxes which had been the subject of controversy but in dropping it the dominion recognized the force of arguments made on several occasions that it was a particularly suitable source of provincial revenue and related closely to the maintenance of provincial highways.
This action by the dominion left only two disputed taxes of any significance, the tax on electricity and that on amusements, including pari-mutuel betting.
With regard to the former, hon. members are aware that there is no electricity tax as such and that what is referred to is merely our ordinary sales tax applied to electricity purchased for domestic use, the previous exemption of this item having been cancelled early in the war. The sales tax is a longstanding and important feature of the dominion's revenue system. Moreover the sales tax on electricity is an indirect tax which could not be levied in any case by provincial governments which are restricted by the constitution to direct taxation. On the other hand it is true to say that the dominion recognizes the importance which the provinces attach to the taxation of electricity because of their interest in rural electrification and their desire to supply electric light and energy to rural dwellers at the lowest possible cost and for this reason a tax on electricity sales is one which the dominion would prefer to avoid if it could afford to do so.
The tax on amusements and pari-mutuel betting is a high-yielding tax, accounting for about $17,000,000 of our revenue at the present time, and is also one which is generally regarded as a desirable tax under present circumstances. Certainly I think hon. members will agree that it would be impossible to raise a corresponding amount of revenue either from income tax or any other field of taxation without producing more harmful economic and social effects. It is also true that this is a tax, the yield of which varies greatly as between the different provinces. If the dominion were to step out of the field, some provinces would not increase their rates of amusement taxation at all, and some might raise their rates but receive very little additional revenue, whilst others might obtain fairly substantial benefits from an increase in rates. On the other hand, I am free to admit that some provinces feel that taxes on amusements and pari-mutuel betting go hand in hand with licensing and regulating functions which provincial governments necessarily perform.
From the correspondence with provincial premiers which has been tabled, the house will be aware that we had been giving the most careful consideration to these remaining minor fields of taxation over a period of many months. They7 were part of a whole series of special taxes which we had been forced to impose during the war emergency and which included a number which we did not regard as likely to continue indefinitely. No government wishes to keep taxes on a moment longer than
Tax Agreements with Provinces

they are needed and the areas where reduction or removal can be effected soundly and equitably are under constant study. As the end of the war receded into the past, we were succeeding more and more in effecting large reductions in our expenditures, and at the same time as a result of the speed and smoothness with which reconversion was being accomplished our revenues were showing a buoyancy to which no one could have looked forward with assurance. It was against this economic and financial background and in the desire to do as much as the dominion government could responsibly do to assure the agreement of all provinces that on April 21 last I wrote to the premier of Nova Scotia outlining the dominion's position in regard to the remaining minor taxes. In regard to the electricity tax I referred in the terms I used a few minutes ago to the dominion's recognition of the interest which provincial governments attach to this tax and concluded with this sentence:
At the moment I cannot go beyond assuring you that the representations of the government of Nova Scotia and those of other provincial governments, respecting the present sales tax on electricity, will be fully considered.
In regard to the amusements tax, I made the following statement:
The dominion recognizes the desire of the provinces to have taxation fields of their own. We are prepared, therefore, to say that in view of the nature of the amusement and pari-mutuel fields, and of the special interest of the provinces in respect thereto, it will be our policy to vacate these fields as soon as circumstances permit.
In a later letter to Premier Macdonald I made it quite clear that in the sentence just, quoted I was stating, that it would be our policy to vacate the amusement and parimutuel fields without compensation as soon as circumstances permit, although this of course did not imply recognition by the dominion of the desirability of any change in the constitutional position respecting taxation.
I have dealt at this length with the question of minor taxes because I wished to remove any cause for misunderstanding or misrepresentation of the dominion position. In addition I trust that this exposition has made it clear that there cannot be found in this question of minor taxes any sufficient basis for failure of any province to enter into an agreement with the dominion.
My third point relates to the magnitude of the annual payments to the provinces. There are some who point out that they are larger than those contained in our original offer to the provinces of August, 1945, larger even than those contained in the budget offer of June 27,

1946, and criticize us for making several improvements in our proposals during the course of the protracted negotiations. We certainly did try to go as far as we could to meet the objections and secure the agreement of all provinces. We admit that the annual payments to be made to provinces under our present offer are substantially higher than those recommended by the Rowell-Sirois royal commission, than those made under the war-time tax agreements, and than those we originally offered. If we can be criticized at all, I think it would be on the ground of the generosity of our proposals. On the other hand, we believe we can justify these agreements, if they result in placing the governments of all provinces in a position to carry out their constitutional functions efficiently and independently, if they safeguard against a scramble amongst ten competing governments for revenues in the field of direct taxation, and if they allow the dominion to develop a sound and efficient tax system calculated to increase employment, production and national income rather than one which acts as a drag upon production.
I believe that those provinces which enter into the agreement will find themselves in an enviable financial position as compared with anything which they have experienced in the past. They will receive revenues from income and corporation taxes and succession duties very much larger than ever before. The guaranteed minimum payment of 8206 million and the estimated adjusted payment for 1947 of over $228 million to which I have already referred compare with a peak yield obtained from the rented tax fields by provincial governments of some $117 million. AVhat is more important in enabling provincial governments to plan programmes of service and expenditure over a period of years is the assurance that for the next five years they will have at least the very high guaranteed revenue from these tax sources, regardless of fluctuations in the national income, regardless of whether the next few years are to bring a business recession. a crop failure or a substantial decline in commodity prices. If, on the other hand, the national income increases and their own population continues to grow, they know also that they are assured of proportionately increased revenues from these tax sources.
Finally, as I said in my budget speech, instead of the provinces which accept the agreement-
-weakening their autonomy or sacrificing any of their constitutional rights, they have merely found a method of utilizing one of these rights, a method of renting instead of cultivating a tax field, whereby they can assure this revenue at generous levels guaranteed against the risks of

Tax Agreements with Provinces
economic adversity and participating also in the profits of growth and prosperity. With this assurance of stable and rising revenues, they are for the first time in a position to plan with courage and confidence and a sense of real independence, programmes for the efficient discharge of their constitutional responsibility.
If I may state this in a different way, we are convinced that acceptance of the proposals will increase rather than diminish the power and prestige of provincial governments because it will enable them to carry out far more effectively and independently the responsibilities which have been assigned to them under our constitution. Nevertheless, it is quite open to any provincial government to hold a contrary view. There is no obligation on any government to enter into the agreement unless it is convinced that such action would be its own best interest. We trust and believe that when the proposals are fully understood, they will commend themselves to all provincial governments. Such general agreement is necessary in order to make possible the achievement of the great national purposes which inspired the comprehensive proposals of August, 1945. The details of our original proposals may of course change as a result of further study or of developing public opinion or of discussion with provincial governments at a general conference which will be necessary before they can be implemented. The proposed contributions which the dominion may be able to make in the field of public investment and social security may, as I have said publicly and as I advised the provinces which were negotiating with us last winter, have to be revised to take into account the substantial increase in the financial payments which' the dominion has now undertaken to make as rental for the tax fields in question. But the main objectives expressed in those proposals remain the guiding objectives of this government. We are hoping that agreement of all provinces may be secured in order that the people of this country may be able to secure the benefits of an efficient and equitable tax system, and in order that all governments may be able to follow policies which promote high employment and high national income, and safeguard against the recurrence of the "boom or depression" experience of the pre-war period.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us this evening is one which has to do with the financial relationships between the provinces and the dominion. This is a country which has a federal system of government, one in which we find a division of government responsibility. We have the central government-in this case the dominion governmentand we have the provincial governments. Each of these governments has certain responsibilities and certain taxing powers.
In Canada the responsibilities are divided between the dominion and provincial jurisdictions. In some cases these responsibilities are not clearly defined. In this country the taxing power is limited in the case of the provinces, and unlimited in the case of the dominion. In other words, there is no taxation field in which the dominion cannot operate. But the provinces are limited to direct taxes.
The bill before us tonight is one to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with the governments of the provinces, agreements in which, in return for compensation, the provinces agree to refrain from levying certain taxes. In other words, the dominion government in this bill asks the provinces to refrain from taxing in certain fields, and for that concession the dominion government undertakes to pay money to the provinces. I believe I have thus correctly described the basic principle in the bill.
The minister has reviewed in brief the history in recent years of dominion-provincial financial relations, and I do not propose to go over that ground again. I did it in a general way on one or two occasions in the last session of parliament, and I do not know that there is anything I can add by way of detail to the statement I then made.
May I at this point refer to one or two comments made by the minister. He referred to the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission, a commission which was appointed by this government ten years ago and which made its report to the government seven years ago. It was a commission the functions of which were to study this question. It did study this question; indeed it studied it thoroughly and for a longer period of time than any other dominion commission of which I am aware. That commission made a most valuable report, one in which is contained what I believe is the fullest and most valuable statement of dominion-provincial affairs made since confederation.
The basic recommendation of that commission was that the provinces of Canada should be aided by the central government on the basis of,fiscal need. What does that mean? In a federal system where we have a central government and, in this instance, nine provincial governments, some of those provincial governments may be operating in an economy which does not give as high a standard of living as is enjoyed by other sections of the nation. That condition is true in Canada. The standard of living varies in different parts and from time to time; and one section may be
Tax Agreements with Provinces

down today or five years from now as compared with the others. In this nation the economy of each province is not exactly a duplicate of the economy of every other province: in fact there are vast differences, so that we find in this nation six different major types of economy.
In the past, some of these provinces have not been able to secure as high a standard of living or of public service as some of the others. In the past, they have been the prairie provinces and the maritime provinces. The result is that in those areas if the people are to have a standard of public service equal to the average in Canada they have to apply ;axation rates much higher than the average taxation rates throughout the rest of the ;ountry.
For many years that condition was permitted to pass by without serious protest, although it is a fact that practically since the time of confederation there have been protests pointing out the inequality of the situation. Any province which has had this condition has considered it a serious matter, but it was not until the depression in the early thirties that the difficulty came prominently to the fore. At that time the provinces in those sections of Canada to which I have referred -and perhaps others-felt they could not face the future and meet their obligations unless these problems were solved.
I believe it will be admitted that it was partly due-and I was going to say largely due-to pressure from certain of those provinces that the dominion consented to have this study made ten years ago. As I have pointed out, the basic recommendation of the royal commission was that the less favoured provinces of Canada should be aided by the central government, the only government able to collect taxes from whatever sources they may be obtained throughout the nation, and that they see to it that the needed moneys will be spent where they are required. The recommendation was that the central government should collect taxes wherever they can be obtained, and that the provinces suffering from poorer economy should be benefited on the basis of fiscal need; that is to the extent of the amount of money necessary to enable those provinces to have the same level of public service as the other provinces have, without having to apply a higher level of taxation.
I need not go into the history of what happened to that report. Everyone knows that in the second year of the war a conference was called and that owing to the objections of certain provinces and the unwillingness of the dominion government to

proceed in the face of those objections, those proposals failed of acceptance. The dominion government came along with another kind of agreement which met these difficulties in somewhat different terms. Those agreements were arranged to terminate at the end of the war.
Then, anticipating the termination of those agreements, the government came forward about two years ago with the plan to which the minister has referred. He has spoken of it as a plan broader in scope than that envisaged iby the Rowell-Sirois commission. It is true that it is broader in scope, much broader. The cost of the plan proposed by the Rowell-Sirois commission cannot in fairness be compared1 on equal terms with the cost of the present proposals. It is just as well, however, to know what the costs were. The minister says ithe plan of 1945 was on a broader scope. The net cost bo the dominion government under the plan proposed by the Rowell-Sirois commission was not $228 million a year; it was but $40 million a year. I am not suggesting that the figures are exactly comparable, but those were the figures they gave. Tonight the minister intimated that the cost of paying the provinces during the war was $117 million, although I had thought the figure was lower than that-some $86 million.
The Rowell-Sirois commission plan was to cost- the dominion $40 million; the wartime tax agreements, as I gathered from the minister, $117 million, although I thought the cost, was less than that; the 1945 proposals, $138 million; the 1946 proposals, $198 million; the present proposals, $228 million. We are in this position then; not only were the 1945 proposals much broader than those of the Rowell-Sirois commission, but the proposals tonight are very much broader at least in cost; they constitute a much greater burden on the Canadian people than the proposals made by the Rowell-Sirois commission; they are very much greater than the payments made by the dominion under the wartime tax agreements; they are very much greater than the proposals brought forward in 1945, and they are very much greater than the proposals brought forward in 1946. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) intimated the other night that if the 1945 proposals were fully implemented they would mean a charge upon this country of $500 million to $600 million a year. Briefly, there is the growth in the development of these projects in recent years.
In my judgment, no good Canadian in any province can oppose payments by the dominion to the provinces on the basis of fiscal

Tax Agreements with Provinces
need. I do not think any provincial government in Canada would oppose that. I do not think any thoughtful student of these matters in. Canada would oppose it. I would think they would all take pride in trying to bring about that measure of equity in this nation. Certainly that is my view and I hope it will be found to be the view of those who sit with me. I am sure it will.
I have not seen certain of the calculations and figures which the minister put on the record tonight, but I am going to refer to them in a moment. But in so far as this measure provides fiscal need for the provinces of Canada, it will receive our support. In so far as it fails to provide fiscal need, the bill is weak and should be remedied. In so far as it provides more than fiscal need, it is not a sound method of financing in Canada.
Does this proposal meet fiscal needs? I will not answer that myself; I will let the government's figures answer it. The 1945 proposals were to cost $138 million; the 1946 proposals, $198 million, and these proposals, a minimum of $206 million, and on the basis of the 1947 figures which the minister gave, $228 million. If in the 1945 proposals the government was planning to meet the fiscal needs of the provinces by providing $138 million, certainly it is paying enough to meet the fiscal needs of the provinces now by providing $228 million which is $90 million more. On that basis I do not think there can be any question but that this plan does meet the fiscal needs of the weaker provinces.
The question now arises: How wise is it to proceed to do more than that? Do ndt misunderstand me; I am not proposing that the provinces of Canada get less than the plan offered now. We are looking at the question of the wisdom of the policy of one government raising money and giving it to other governments to spend. To the extent that it is necessary to meet fiscal need, I will support it and I think every good Canadian will support it; but to the extent that it goes beyond that, I ask this question: Is that sound fiscal policy? Is that sound financial policy? I am not going to depend upon my own opinion in that matter, I am going to quote what another authority had to say several years ago on this question. I should like to quote from page 316 of Hansard of February 21, 1929. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking at that time, had this to say:
I believe that everyone who has given any attention to public finance will agree that it is a thoroughly vicious system to have one body raise taxes and another body expend the money thus secured. In other words, give to the provinces these grants from the federal treasury,
without their being obliged to raise the money themselves by taxation, and you will not get, with respect to expenditure, that careful supervision which would be exercised if the provinces themselves were obliged to raise the money in the first instance. It is a bad system, a thoroughly vicious system, and that is the reason wby the present administration has been seeking to put an end to a system that grew up at a time when the country was in the throes of war or had to meet a post-war situation-a system which, had it been permitted to develop, would have become thoroughly destructive of anything in the shape of economy w'ith respect to the expenditure of the people's money.
The same position was taken later on, on April 3, 1930. The same authority, the present Prime Minister of Canada, had this to say, as reported on page 1237 of Hansard:
When on a previous occasion we were discussing this matter of grants from one treasury to another, I said I thought it was an unsound principle; in fact, I think I used the expression that it was a vicious principle to have one body raise the taxes and another body spend the people's moneys thus raised. Is there any hon. member who will disagree with me in that statement?
Those are not my words; they are the words of the Prime Minister. That question is his question, not mine. Then he went on to answer it as follows:
There is none. That is the extent of the statement I made. I was referring to a principle of financing, speaking simply in relation to what is sound and what is unsound in financing. Anyone interested in financing, whether of a municipality, a province, a dominion, an empire, or a league of nations, will, I think, admit it is unwise, an unsound, a wrong principle for one body to have to do with raising the taxes and another to be concerned with the spending of the money so raised, that other body not having to account to the representatives of those *who have paid the taxes.
As I said, this measure, in so far as it provides fiscal need to the provinces of Canada will, I hope, receive the support of every right-thinking Canadian. This measure does that; but I criticize it on several grounds. I criticize it, first, because the government goes at the question of solving this problem in the wrong way, a way which makes for disunity in Canada. It approaches the provinces one by one. It has now got seven provinces in out of nine. These seven provinces represent only about one-third of the tax-paying part of Canada and only a little more than one-third of the population of Canada. Of the money that is being used by the government for this purpose, two-thirds or three-quarters of it come from those provinces which, under the present arrangement are receiving no benefits. The point I am now making is that the approach is wrong; the government, as I said, is going at the problem in the ivrong way. It is an
Tax Agreements with Provinces

approach which makes for disunity. Was there ever any question in anybody's mind that when a proposal like this came forward, a proposal in which the government of Canada said to the provinces, "we will get two-thirds or three-quarters of this money from two provinces and give it to you", those six or seven provinces would eventually accept? None at all. That is my first criticism. Is it a healthy condition that we should have seven provinces accepting this, seven which get much more than they could raise from these revenues in their own jurisdiction, and two not having it; yet paying much of what the others get? I ask, is that a healthy state in this nation? Should we not be applying ourselves seriously to trying to solve these problems without having such a situation as this arise?
My second criticism is this. In a federal state this policy of the government goes a long way toward centralizing taxation powers. Whether that is good or bad there can be no question of the facts. That is what it does. We have admitted that it does secure a small measure of equality, having regard to the responsibility of the provincial governments. This measure helps certain provincial governments; but it does not help correct inequalities in the economy of the different parts of the nation. It helps governments improve their problems with respect to public services. My immediate criticism is that in a federal state, with each government having to raise its own revenues, this plan goes a long way toward centralizing taxing power in Canada. The government asks the provinces to give up their powers to tax. The government says, "We will give you money back for this concession; we will give you more than you raise yourselves". But the fact is, that having been done, the powers of taxation rest in this government, not with the provinces.
The minister talks about "renting" taxes. It is more than renting taxes; it is asking the provinces to give up constitutional rights.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext: Renting rights.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext:
My third criticism is that in a federal state-and that is what ours is- this plan fails to give to the provinces any clear field of taxation of their own; it does not give them even any minor fields. There is not a single taxation field into which the dominion cannot go. There is scarcely a single field into which the dominion has not gone. I do not think there is a single field into which the dominion has said that it would not go. It has left some fields temporarily; it may stay out for a while, but it has not said it would

stay out indefinitely. It does not say that the provinces can have any small taxation field of their own from which the dominion would keep away.
My fourth criticism is that the government's procedure, as it worked out, has failed to achieve continuance of plans for dominion-provincial conferences. That is a serious criticism. The government may say, "Well, we tried and we failed; we have not any hope of getting anywhere if we call another conference," and the other folks will give their answer and say, you were too rigid, and so on. If we are to wait until these problems are easy to solve before we are willing to sit down together and face hard difficulties and overcome 'them, we are going to be a long time in getting a better country. My criticism is that the government has failed to achieve a continuance of dominion-provincial conference. In a federal state that is a serious condition of affairs. Here we are working together, dominion and provinces; sometimes our jurisdictions overlap; sometimes they do not, but they are always closely related. The healthiest condition this nation could have would be for the dominion to have regular conferences wi'th the provinces. I feel that, to the extent powers are centred here in Ottawa and used here, we are arriving at a dangerous situation where a few men can make major decisions on important matters. This nation will be a healthier place if the dominion and the several provinces were to sit down together more frequently. If the provinces are not well informed, inform them. But do not try to order them. Inform them ahd educate them. Geit them to come together with the dominion. But I am not suggesting that the provinces need education.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext: I think they do.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext: All right; name which ones.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext: I will name them.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext:
My fifth criticism is that this policy has resulted in delaying certain social security, health and public investment policies which were well received across this nation when they were put forward by the experts of the government some -two or three years ago. This government brought forth these policies and said they were good. They said, we will put them into effect if the provinces will agree. It turns out that these policies will cost the nation $500 or $600 million a year when they are implemented. The government now comes forward and says, only seven provinces having agreed, it cannot bring

Tax Agreements with Provinces
forward these policies which it said would help this nation head off a depression in the future. It is said that a depression is in the offing and these things would help avoid it. Yet, the government fails to come forward with these measures itself and it fails to call the provinces together to tiy to get a plan to put them into effect. I say their plan has delayed the bringing forward of these policies of social security, health and public investment-public works or whatever you like to call them-policies aimed to correct certain social inequities in Canada and at the same time help to head off the danger of a recession.
My sixth criticism is that the plan abandons the principle of fiscal needs. The minister referred to that. He said that it is different from fiscal need. He said that his plan had covered the principle of fiscal need; but, Mr. Speaker, this plan'is not a plan of fiscal need; neither is this plan on the basis of equal per capita payment; this plan is the result of going at things piecemeal and having to consider something different for each province. This plan is the result of going at this thing piecemeal; having got three provinces to agree at first, the government found that British Columbia wanted more and they had to give more to get British Columbia in. The government having got British Columbia in, the other provinces felt they had a grievance and came here and the government felt it had to give them more.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext: We think we did all right in British Columbia.

maintopic: CALCULATION OF ADJUSTED ANNUAL PAYMENT FOR 1947
speechtext:
Finally, as the minister said tonight, the seventh province has come in. Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say this to the minister who has introduced the bill. He put on the record certain calculations, certain figures, which none of us have seen. I can complete my remarks tonight at this stage and be through, but I am wondering whether that will accomplish most in the way of expediting the debate. We are not planning to have many speakers on this side. I should like to deal with the matter as fully as needed and as fairly and frankly as I see it. If the government is not ready to go on with anything else and wishes me to complete my remarks tonight I will do so but if I do, and I find in the record something that we have not seen, or something that is new, or something that needs to be answered, we shall have to deal with it as necessary in committee of the whole. We can do that, and from the point of view of the opposition, perhaps from a purely political point of view, that would
be the better thing for us to do. I am willing to go on and finish my remarks tonight, or I am willing to leave the matter over in order to see what there is that is new in what the minister has put on the record, and then conclude tomorrow. I am not asking any favour of the minister. If he feels that it will expedite the work of the house in dealing with this particular matter to go on with other matters now, that can be done, but if he prefers to have me conclude now I can follow that course.

speechtext: I am willing to meet my hon. friend's convenience, but I do not think he will find in the tables I placed on Hansard tonight anything that contains new material. It is largely informative, to show how the increased commitments are calculated on the basis of the gross national production, set out in detail, the minimum payments on the latest population figures we have for the various provinces, and so on. But if my hon. friend prefers to adjourn the debate and go on later, I would not object. As I say, however, he will not find that the tables I have put on Hansard tonight will supply any material for which he would have any particular need for the purposes of his statement.

The house again in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The committee is considering item 551, national defence.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was reading a letter which appeared in Maclean's magazine, and I should like to finish it now:
Before the price to be offered to each owner was finally decided upon, each property was reviewed by a board of appraisers, made up of those listed herein, when the soldiers' settlement representatives appeared before the board to discuss and justify their valuation of each property. All were treated alike, tbfre was no coercion, no favouritism, and in my estimation, never was an expropriation more carefully planned and more equitably settled than this undertaking.
Supply-National Defence

If the owner thought the amount offered to him was not fair, and he had even the slightest reason for his contention, the property was reappraised by two soldiers' settlement representatives, and adjustments made if found warranted.
How you can print such a report without fully investigating the facts, does not seem in keeping with your usual standard. Surely you do not print everything any crackpot says, and I suggest a little more vigilance on the part of your editors would keep out such erroneous reporting.
It seems to me that in a spirit of justice you should rectify this statement by printing the facts in your next issue.
Yours very truly,
Westmount Realties Company,
J. W. Rankin, Vice-president.
That is a letter which appeared in Maclean's magazine. I may say that many of the statements in that letter were entirely wrong. The letter may express the writer's point of view, but it was certainly not the point of view of the settlers who had resided in that, area for thirty or forty years, and some of them perhaps longer.
While I do not wish to tire the committee, I should like to read a letter which I received from one of the residents in that area, a man who had lived there for thirty-five years and who perhaps knew the conditions in that district better than any of those the government had in there. The letter is from a man named Philip E. Birtwistle, a resident of Medicine Hat, who had resided in the area. The letter is dated June 21, 1946, and reads: An item appeared in Maclean's magazine of March 15, referring to the British block and the injustice of the settlement v7ith the expropriated residents. It evoked a letter from a Mr. Rankin of Montreal, which appeared in Maclean's of June 1, in which he says the article is misleading and makes several statements in support of his contention. I have written a reply to his letter, refuting his statements. I am enclosing a copy of the letter as it will probably be a month before it appears in print. I also enclose a resolution from the Redcliff town council. Plenty of supporting evidence can be produced should the case be reopened.
This is what this gentleman has to say. He s writing to the editor, Maclean's magazine, Toronto, Ontario:
^ Dear Sir:	I have read the article in Cross
Country of Maclean's, March 15 and a letter from a Mr. Rankin of Montreal, commenting on it. As the first article was a fair, but by no means complete statement of the case, I did not feel called upon to amplify it. But, as Mr. Rankin's letter may prejudice the chances of a reopening of the case, I would like to answer, and refute, the statements he made.
As a farmer in the block I was served with a notice of expropriation by an R.C.M.P. officer, not by mail, and told I must get out by a certain date. There was no question of negotiating agreements, but, being dissatisfied with the  .	,
amount allotted to my partner and myself, I saw Colonel Gibson, who was in authority, who did not think it necessary to interview me in an office, but did his business with me in the lobby of the court house, standing up. He refused to discuss the settlement in detail, or to give me a detailed, itemized statement. He said I could accept or let it go to the exchequer court, but, he added, by the time the exchequer court settled it, the buildings and other improvements, which we were to be allowed to remove, would be gone. I asked him where they would be and he replied, "Oh, just smashed up and got out of the way."
The statement that all interested parties accepted the terms offered, although apparently correct, is actually wrong. Two factors forced the farmers to accept, although most of them tried to get better terms with little or no success. The first factor was, that it was a war measure. We were told, and it was correct, that the area was needed for the prosecution of the war. To buck it or delay it would be unpatriotic and we definitely agreed with this.
The second factor was economic. The farmers had just been through the worst depression in history, with prices for farm products at an all-time low. They were making out all right, but were unable to leave their homes and finance themselves until the exchequer court settled the case. How could they set about securing another location, purchase another farm, move on to it and wait a year for returns from it, without any settlement of their holdings? What would the majority of them live on, for perhaps a year, before the exchequer court settled it, while their crop was in the ground and they could not harvest it? Although not legally forced to accept, actually they had no alternative.
The next statement, that, "of 275 interested parties, more than half had found it impossible to make a living." is another half-truth. There were actually 126 families residing in the block at the time of the expropriation. Like all such pioneer settlements, many left at different times for many different reasons. Some left for their health as the climate did not suit them. Some were unable to stand the grind of pioneering. Some left because of the distance from town, and the depression and low prices was a main factor in forcing many away. But the 126 that remained were doing all right, many of them were engaged in large scale farming, with power equipment, and stock as a sideline, and. had they been left there, would have made very good and substantial gains in the past five years of rising prices.	The last statement, referring to the
delegation who wished to be included in the block, is on a par with the other statements. They knew nothing of the prices, good or bad, but as their grazing and other holdings would be seriously reduced by the closing of the block and, as this would cut out a large part of their income, they considered they would be unable to carry on with their diminished holdings.
I enclose a statement of the holdings of my partner and myself, and the amount we received, which I believe is fairly average, and it may be appended if the editor thinks fit to do so. I could amplify this further but I think the above is sufficient to show we have a good case for reconsideration.
That is a letter from a resident of that block, who lived there for many years and

Supply-National Defence
made a success of farming in that dry area. I may say that the settlement in this Bing-ville district was one of the happiest communities in Alberta. Many social events were held there where the people got together. They were the ones who had been left there while the others moved out, and the settlement they got was entirely inadequate.
Carried:
It will be carried when I am through.
Is that a promise?
