I want to put on Hansard a statement regarding the settlement made with this farmer and his partner, and what he got for 640 acres of land with buildings and everything. This is a statement of holdings in the spring of 1941: land, 640 acres, full title, unencumbered and all taxes fully paid; 1.280 acres under crop lease from provincial government; 320 acres under grazing lease from provincial government; house, IS by 24, two story with verandah and porch; granaries, capacity, 10,000 bushels-five, 12 by 14; one, 12 by 16; one, 18 by 24; barns-one 18 by 30; one, 18 by 28, with lean-to 24 by 16; garages-one, 12 by 20; one, 10 by 16; blacksmith shop, chicken house and coal shed; fence, five miles, 850 posts, 12 miles barbed wire; two wells, one dam and two miles of graded road, built by them at their own expense. In addition to that, they had 620 acres seeded to wheat in that year. For those holdings they received the sum of $5,700. After a period of forty years, does anyone consider that to be a fair settlement? I should think not. I am afraid that those farmers are not in the same class as those whom we were discussing in this house just a little while ago, where one could go to the government and get a better settlement, and then another come along. These farmers were not in that class. They had to accept what was offered to them; and, being good patriotic citizens, they did that and assisted in the war effort all they could.
I feel that more consideration should be given to them and I see no reason why the case should not be reopened. I know of one farmer in particular who had gone through a period of bad years, when he had no crop for six or seven years. By 1941 he was just getting back on his feet and had a nice herd of cattle. He was running about 125 head of cattle and about forty head of horses. He was too old to go out and start up in a new community. Therefore he had to dispose of his
stock and everything and move into the city of Medicine Hat. Everything he got for his holdings is now pretty well gone, because of the increased cost of living and many other items. I hope the minister and the government will see fit to reopen this case and see if these farmers cannot get a better settlement and if a readjustment cannot be allowed on many of the settlements which were made. I should like to know what the government intends to do about this matter. There is no use in letting it slip along. The parliamentary assistant to the minister is here and he should be able to let me know what the government intends to do about it.

speakeroldname: Mr. HUGUES LAPOINTE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can only say that I shall be pleased to bring the matter to the minister's attention for his consideration; but, as the hon. member knows very well, it has been considered from time to time. Up to this date it has been considered that the settlement was adequate and no decision has been made to reopen the case. I shall again draw the matter to the minister's attention.

Can the parliamentary
assistant say when the consideration will be given and how many applied for consideration?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It has I know, been given just lately. As soon as the estimates are through, I shall be very glad to have the matter reopened.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant four or five questions, and in doing so I would not want to be understood as trying to injure the defence forces in any way. The present position of Canada is such that we must do everything possible to help the men who are trying to give us efficient defence forces. We have moved from the bush league into the big league in world affairs, and from now on for all time we must be prepared to face this question, not only of whether we vare able to defend ourselves, but also of whether we are able to do our share in building up an effective world police organization.
The first question I would ask the minister, who has now come into the house, has to do with the trained field force, about which very little has been said today. When the former minister of national defence laid down the policy in this house on October 16, 1945, he dealt fully with this field force. He was giving the two main elements of the post-war army. In the first place, he referred to the part-time reserve army, and then went on to
Supply-National Defence

deal with what we call the permanent force. At page 1135 of Hansard for October 16, 1945, he said:
The second will be the permanently employed active force, whose duty it will be to assist in the training and administration of the reserve army and to supply the necessary staffs, services and scientific research and development personnel, augmented by a small formation of essential field units. This formation will be maintained as a trained field force, fully epuipped, ready to meet whatever commitments may arise. Until we know more about our international obligations and consequent requirements, these active force units will be retained as a minimum and would be subject to whatever expansion might later be required in the light of any obligations which we might accept to assist in maintaining the peace of the world. Preliminary estimates indicate that the numbers involved in the active permanently employed force will be between 20,000 and 25,000 all ranks.
We were given to understand at that time that this trained field force would be, in effect, a brigade group, with infantry, armour, artillery, engineers and so on; that it would be a field force ready to operate as such. A year later, in October, 1946, the same defence minister, the present Minister of Finance, was questioned about Canada's peace-time forces while he was visiting in Victoria. At that time the Russians were demanding a general reduction in armaments, and the minister was asked what Canada would do about reducing her armaments. His answer was to this effect, that Canada's peace-time forces were so small there was nothing to cut. That was the substance of his statement at that time. Then in January, 1947, the present minister announced a twenty-five per cent cut. I should like to know what has happened to this trained field force, whether it is still in existence or just what has happened to it.
Then I wish to ask a question in the same connection about the reserve army. In the statement on October 16, 1945, the former minister laid great stress on the role of the reserve army, and referred to it as-
. . . this important force which will form the background of any possible future military endeavour . . .
Today w'e find much the same statement made by the minister as the fifth paragraph of the programme he presented, in these words:
Development of reserve forces of an age and with educational and physical standards and training approximating those of the active forces competent to go to sea, take the field or fly.
Yet this afternoon he said the men in the reserve forces would get only fourteen days of training in a year, though some groups such as trade groups may get extra training. In the face of a programme of that kind I would ask him to explain how it is going to be

possible to build up a reserve army with standards of training approximating those of the active forces, competent to go to sea, take the field or fly. Two years ago we warned the then minister that he would have to give a very strong lead at once if he wished to build up a reserve army in Canada. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Gazette, published in the minister's own city, dated June 28, just a few days ago-

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Not my paper, though.
Well, the minister will agree that it is a good paper.
I do not think I agree with that in regard to its news items or its editorials.
This is a news item, and I do not think he will question it.
I certainly do.

The heading is:
Black Watch only military unit to arrange for summer camp.
All other reserve bodies are much below strength due to general lack of public interest, is claim.
The article goes on to say this, about this famous regiment:
The Black Watch (RHR) of Canada will be the only military unit in this area to attend summer reserve camp in a body this year, it was learned yesterday. The Black Watch will spend a week end in July at Farnham.
Because of a general lack of interest in reserve army training since the end of the war, all units are very much below strength.
I would ask the minister to deal with those two points, the matter of the field force and the possibility of building up a fully trained reserve army on the basis of a few days' training a year, as he announced this afternoon.

In regard to the last remark of the hon. member, concerning a quotation from the Montreal Gazette, I should say that is the kind of incorrect editorializing that frequently appears in some newspapers in Canada. That article is not in accordance with the facts as I know them. Other units are going to train; and the kind of training provided, as I have said, is on a scale never before equalled in Canada. Provision is made for thirty days training for the quota of 30,000, and, in addition, fourteen days at camp plus fifteen days additional training for tradesmen. I would ask any hon. member who has had any experience with the reserve forces to say whether anything has

Supply-National Defence
ever before been done to this degree in Canada. With regard to the statement about the twenty-five per cent cut-
If I may ask a question, surely that 30,000 covers all three services, not just one?
This is just for the army alone.
Thirty thousand for the army alone?

Yes; and, with regard to the 25 per cent cut, may I say that is something which I believe was developed out of the newspapers. What has happened is that for the purposes of the armed forces this year we are recruiting only up to 75 per cent of the established strengths of the active forces. There has been no change in their establishment. That applies also to the brigade groups. It is quite right for the hon. member to ask about the status of his brigade group. It does not yet exist as a fighting unit fit to take the field at any moment. That work is still in progress. The men are still being trained and organizational work is being done. In it at the present time there is a total of 192 officers and 1,952 men.
What would be the establishment for that field force?

A brigade group has always been a fairly indefinite term. I believe the idea in mind at the time it was first suggested was that it should amount to something of the magnitude of about 5.000 officers and men.
That is the figure I had in mind.
And I believe, on the 75 per cent strength, it would be of the magnitude of 3,541 officers and men.

Does the minister not think it would be wise to carry out the original policy, recruit this brigade group up to strength, and keep it up to strength and trained as a fighting unit? As I understand it, they are now scattered all the way from Esquimalt to Sydney or Halifax. Would it not be wise to relax the 75 per cent rule in respect of that field force, bring it up to strength, and have a first-class and efficient fighting brigade group in Canada?

The hon. member's question is a difficult one to answer because it depends upon a great many technical and strategical considerations, with which I am not competent to deal. But I should think that once one regards the armed forces of Canada from what I believe is the right point of view
at the present time, that is as a training force for future staff officers and leaders, and for the reserve forces of Canada, then I should think the wisdom of keeping constantly mobilized and ready for action anything in the nature of a brigade group in one place would be a mistake.
It all depends upon time, circumstances, dangers and everything else. Given the present development of weapons

and I say that advisedly in view of what was said this afternoon -we can take care of anything that happens in Canada in the immediate future. Given another kind of development of weapons and technique, that might not be adequate. But for the time being I believe our primary purpose should be to develop staff officers, officers training establishments, depots, technicians and tradesmen, as well as trained personnel who are competent to provide the nucleus for anything that might happen in the future.
That can only mean, then, that the government has now abandoned the policy announced in 1945.
No.
Yes, it does.
It has to be related to the time.

The policy then as stated by the Minister of National Defence was perfectly clear, and here it is:
This formation will be maintained as a trained field force fully equipped, ready to meet whatever commitments may arise.
The minister's statement tonight means that we are reverting to the days of the thirties, when we are using our permanent force for training and staff work. Obviously there is a change of policy, and I do not think it is a proper change. I suggest, however, that the committee can see for itself what is meant. The minister cannot rise in his place now and say that the policy he has announced is anything but an absolute turning away from the policy announced on October 16, 1945, with regard to the field force.
It is a question of time and of the wise spending of such resources as we have.
Of course things are more serious now than they were then.

Well, they may be. The fact is that I believe we can take care of things as they exist today in Canada. We are not abandoning, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South, the idea of a brigade group which might be ready to take the field if that were necessary. That
532S
Supply-National Defence

has not been abandoned at all; it is being organized, trained and worked at. On the other hand, we are concentrating our attention equally on the other necessities of defence: how much we do of each depends, in part, on the flow of training schedules, the flow of recruits and on other considerations which vary from time to time, as well as on the necessities of the case.
As I see it at the present time, we are going sufficiently fast with both, provided that during the current year we can encourage, with the support of hon. members and other public-spirited people throughout the country, young Canadians to go into the armed forces in sufficient numbers to bring them up to the strength authorized. That requires some additional enlistments, particularly in connection with the army. They are coming along; and in order to secure them we are putting on the campaign next September to which I have already referred.

I believe the minister would find that one of the greatest attractions to the young men of this country would be the possibility of enlisting in a crack field force where they would receive the most modern training. We understood, in 1945 for example, that the whole field force were to be trained as paratroopers. If the minister were to set up something of that type he would find that young Canadians would respond quickly and would make the finest force in the world. But I say to him it will be very difficult to build up a first-class force if these units are to be scattered right across Canada, away under strength, and simply doing sentry duty or routine training of one kind or another. I would ask the minister to turn that over in his mind between sessions.

That is one of the difficulties any country the size of Canada has in apportioning its armed forces among three services over a great area. I appreciate the point the hon. member made, because that is one thing that gave us much concern. I must point out, however, that all the men entering the armed forces receive the most modern training and that very few of them are engaged in sentry duty or anything of that kind.
I meant duties of that sort.

I understand that. But in anything of that kind our aim is to have as much as possible of the work of security guards, fire-fighters, clerks, mess orderlies, cooks and the like done by civilians, so that all in the armed forces will be trained fighting soldiers. Whether one of those soldiers is at any given moment made part of a brigade

group, which is a fighting operational unit, or is made part of a training establishment in one of the training camps in Canada probably matters very little from the point of view of that man's efficiency. We hope to have everyone efficient and we believe they are. It may be that we shall find that to isolate them in brigade groups doing nothing but operational exercises will not be the best way to keep up their keenness and that they should be associated with men in training in other fields. The whole operation and plan will have to be worked out, and I think it is being done in a sensible way.

I suggest to the minister that he have some special name for that brigade group; make it a corps d'elite. I think, if it Were permitted to train in different parts of Canada at different times he would find that the effect would be most beneficial both to the reserve army and to the active army.
My next question has to do with these more modern weapons of war. This morning the minister referred to atomic bombs, jet-propelled planes, rockets and higher speed submarines as being the principal new weapons introduced near the end of the recent war. He referred also to chemical and bacteriological agents. During his statement this afternoon he explained that the jet-propelled planes were on order from Great Britain. Has the Canadian government taken any steps to invite the British government to send their airmen here to train in jet-propelled planes? I believe they have the greatest difficulty in training over the United Kingdom because they hardly get started before they are over the sea. Out on the prairies we have the air fields, the distances and the suitable weather, and it seems to me thait it would be appropriate for Canada to take a lead in setting up some type of commonwealth air training plan for the training of personnel in the handling of these jet-propelled planes. The same thing is true in connection with training in the use of mechanized units by the army. Has Canada taken any steps to arrange for this kind of training to be done in Canada? The Ottawa Citizen of June 14 contained an article headed, "See Canada as key in era of superweapons. Even atom mist range in northland reported." This was a dispatch from London, and referring to Canada it said:
For Canada this scheme is believed by these sources to envisage the setting up of an atomic range in -the frozen northland on the lines of the Australian rocket range in the bush country. Here experiments with radio-active "clouds" could be carried out in safety. This was forecast for the near future

Supply-National Defence
Will the minister state whether anything has been done along the lines I suggest?

There is a great deal of misunderstanding about jet propelled planes. I certainly am far from being an expert in this or any other military field, except perhaps the six-inch howitzer which is long obsolete, but I understand that flying a jet propelled plane does not entail any particularly new problem. I am informed by my advisers that they are as easy to fly, if not easier, than many of the later type planes in the last war and that their landing speeds are not very different from those of other planes. Apart from their higher speed! and probably cheaper cost of production, they are not very different from ordinary planes.
We have not had any request from the United Kingdom that we should provide training fields for flyers along the lines of the British commonwealth air training plan, nor have we had- any request for training in mechanized warfare. I would think that the United Kingdom had ample facilities for both types of training. On the other hand, we exchange staff officers and technicians every now and then; we exchange information and have the closest kind of cooperation with the United Kingdom as we have with the United States. There is nothing additional that appears to be necessary to be done in this connection at this time. It has not been suggested by anyone with army experience. Our cooperation with what I described as other like-minded nations is free and frank and leads to greater efficiency on both sides.

Would this suggestion, if carried out, not help our own air men? Would there be any objection from the Canadian point of view to carrying out a plan of that type? The training would be done under the department and the Canadian authorities.

I am not sure how that would work out and I would have to discuss it with my colleagues. If it seems to be desirable from the air force point of view, then it would have to be considered from the point of view of policy and so on. I am not in a position to give a reply offhand. I can assure my hon. friend and the committee that there is the closest cooperation with regard to staff work, instructors and technicians.

In recent weeks there has been considerable publicity with regard to the acquisition of United States equipment. There have been discussions in the United States congress about putting through a statute allowing them to help other nations in the Americas 83166-340
to equip their forces. According to newspaper articles, it would appear that Canada can acquire only used equipment or equipment which has been discarded by the United States forces. Is that correct, and can the minister outline the situation with regard to this equipment?

The bill referred to by the hon. member was introduced in the United States congress quite recently and is still tinder consideration, not having as yet been adopted. It is purely facilitative or enabling legislation. It would permit the President of the United States or the administration to make arrangements with any of the American states to provide them with equipment or assistance with regard to defence. So far that bill has not been passed. Whether or not it is passed is, of course, for the United1 States congress to say. If it were passed it would, I think, within its terms, and probably hon. members will agree that it might, enable the United States to make equipment available to us on any terms that were agreed to by the administration. We, however, have a quite different arrangement with the United States, that expressed in the Ogdensburg declaration of August 19, 1940, and now carried forward by the declaration of the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States of America on February 12, 1947. Under this w.e agreed to cooperate with regard to the defence of this continent. All hon. members are familiar with the provisions of that declaration.
So far, with regard to equipment we have bought from the United States with United States dollars the equipment we have .felt we needed, and we have got it on terms that have been worked1 out by agreement between the two countries. There has been no suggestion that we get only used equipment. That is not so. We get what we want when they have what we want and what we cannot make ourselves, and we have so far paid for it.
Then we really do not need this enabling statute which is before the United States congress.

So far we have not used it. It has not been in force and we have not used' it. We cannot see everything that will happen in the future, but so far this measure, which is HR-3836, and which was introduced in the house of representatives on June 13, 1947, has not been enacted. It has not been applied, and so far Canada has got along under a totally different arrangement.

I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to Canada's com-

Supply-National Defence

mitments to the united nations. In his statement this morning he said that Canada's defence force may be required:
1.	To defend Canada against aggression;
2.	To assist the civil power in maintaining law and order, within the country;
3.	To carry out any undertakings which by our own voluntary act we may assume in cooperation with friendly nations or under any effective plan of collective action under the united nations.
Can the minister give us any idea of. what sort of assistance Canada would be expected to furnish to the united nations? Within the last few days proposals have been put in to the security council for a world force. Does the minister know where Canada fits into that picture? I see that on April 12 of this year he ventured into print on the question at Winnipeg. That is a long way from Ottawa and the quotation may not be correct, or the minister may have been enjoying the western air out there, as we westerners all hope to to do in a few days. The heading is:
Canada may send troops overseas for peace force.
The press dispatch is dated April 12 and reads as follows:
Canada is prepared to send troops overseas to take part in an international peace force should one be established, Defence Minister Claxton said here. He is in Winnipeg on a tour of western Canada.
Can the minister give us some further statement with regard to that position?

With regard to what I said at Winnipeg, it was just the same as what I said today; it. is the same as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said on previous occasions, namely, that any arrangements for our contribution to a united nations force would have to be agreed to in accordance with the charter of the united nations by the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament. I said that in Winnipeg; I cannot say anything different; it is a fact, both from the charter and from the realities of Canadian policy. If the hon. member had quoted all of what I had said-
That is all they printed. I do not know what else the minister said.

Then the newspaper may have left out something of what I said. The report that I saw of what I said at Winnipeg was completely correct; that is, that it was qualified in the sense in which I have just qualified it, and the only sense in which it could be qualified; that is, that we will agree to use our forces in conjunction with those of the united nations by act of our own parlia-

ment after they have seen what the situation is and learned what it is. I could not say anything more than that, but certainly we are not committing ourselves in advance to any blank cheque. As to what we may be expected to commit ourselves to, I can only say that, as a fairly realistic people, we would like to see what it is before I can give an answer to my hon. friend.
Can the minister give us any idea at the present time?

There is not the slightest idea in anyone's mind as to what it might be. The discussions of a possible united nations force have certainly not yet reached that level; but I would think myself that whatever it might be it would be well within our capacity to give.

One final subject, the ques- * tion of civil defence. The minister listed as his eleventh objective today:
Organization of government departments and civilian agencies capable of putting into immediate effect a plan for civil defence.
What is in mind in that connection? Such a plan necessitates support of civilian bodies all over Canada, and that support cannot be gained in a hurry. They have to be sold on the need for some such organization, and there is a great deal of preliminary work to do before such an organization is made effective. Has the department taken any steps at all, or what is the picture at the present time? In April of this year, Colonel W. W. Goforth, retiring deputy director of defence research gave a five-point programme in Vancouver to prepare Canadians against possible atomic assault. He was not speaking officially for the Department of National Defence, but he listed five interesting ways of building up this special defence. They were as follows:
,1 That the three forces "will so combine and organize their strength within the limited resources assigned them that they may provide efficient early warning, interception and close support services to guard our great cities and vital centres from the first waves of enemy attack."	.
2.	That each community of 50,000 population and' over, "encouraged and guided by .provincial authorities," study the results of atomic destruction as now known and * translate these into amendments of greater dispersion, even into their system of granting building permits relative to the zone of danger."
3.	That professional societies such as the Engineering Institutes of Canada, Royal Architectural Institute of Canada, Canadian Medical Association, and others "study and devise codes and simplified instructions for use by their members in local surveys and in expert counsel to local authorities."

Supply-National Defence
Mind you, all these are startling proposals.
4.	That individual industries and public utilities start reviewing ways and means for achieving gradual dispersion "but with comparable productivity and economy."
5.	Not an immediate problem but "one needing serious preliminary attention within the next five years," is the question of "a revived and greatly-strengthened air raid precaution (ARP) organization with gradually developed plans for mass evacuation and billeting of nonessential population from the larger cities.
The minister should give the committee some statement with regard to this question of civil defence. His department is obviously concerned about it, and there should be something more definite than statements such as that given by Colonel Goforth. It is an alarming statement which may be a thoroughly wise warning. Will the minister make a statement with regard to civil defence?

Colonel Goforth spoke for himself. With regard to what I had -in mind when I suggested that, I can say at once that what we intend to do is to have the Department of National Defence and other departments concerned work out plans which might be put into effect progressively as the threat grew. We certainly have nothing in mind along the lines of the suggestion made by my hon. friend.
Carried.

There is quite a chorus of "carried" from the other side. If hon. members had the privilege of seeing the list of speakers, as I have had, they would not call "carried" for a while yet, because there are quite a few. Incidentally, I am not one of those who clamour for a hurried-up closing. I never did believe that we would finish on the 12th of July and I do not believe it. There are too many matters to be discussed. Those hon. members on the other side who shout "carried" should exercise some influence in their party caucus to have some of the important legislation -introduced in the early part of the session. If they had done that, instead of fiddling a month away in February, possibly it would not be necessary for them to join the chorus shouting "carried." However, let them have a good time.
I wish to compliment the minister on the clarity of his statement this morning. It was one of the clearest and most definite we have had on this or any other government subject since I have been a member of this house. I have not a copy of the statement, but I listened carefully, and the Evening Journal prints a copy of the fourteen points which the minister announced this morning. I presume that copy is correct. There are one or 83166-340J
two of the points that I might feel like questioning, but in the main I agree with them.
This afternoon the hon. member for Trinity spent a little time in extolling the value of the particular branch of the forces in which he had such distinguished service. I do not blame him for doing so, nor do I blame some other members who have promoted the particular branches of the service in which they were engaged; but I would remind them, without drawing comparisons as to which branch is better or worse, or which is more valuable, that we old mud-sluggers, the PJB.I.'s did our job too. The others might not have done so valuable a job had not our service played its part too. That is not an odious comparison. It is simply a reminder that whether you fly or tramp around in the mud to your waist you are doing the best you can.
How about a little more pay for the infantry?
Now you are talking. I suggest that it be brought up to the others. I will support the hon. member there, even though I may not succeed.
They get the same rate.
I am glad to hear that. All the way through, considering allowance?
Oh, yes, all three services.

I am glad to hear that. The hon. member for Selkirk says we joined too late, or too soon rather. We were born thirty years too soon. I want to point out that this group do recognize the need for a defence board. Once in a while some unfortunate statements are made in the house, possibly in consequence of a little stir-up, but I do not think the C.C.F. group need take a back seat to any other group, and again that is not an odious comparison. We all made what contribution we could during the war. There may be a difference in policy and in ideas from time to time as to when is the strategic time for Canada to enter war, but I do not think there will ever come a time when Canada is at war that those of our group, and those associated with us in the country, will not make their full contribution in man and woman-power and in other ways when they are called upon to do so. Whether there are more from one group or from another represented in the military forces, I do not know, and I do not see much difference in proportion to membership in the house.
Certainly we recognize the need for, and we-should like to see, a well-balanced military establishment, and that is one thing about
Supply-National Defence

the minister's statement that I liked. It appears at least that he has a good idea of how to bring about a well-balanced and well-coordinated military establishment. That means not only well-trained but well-equipped troops, and I hope he is successful, because, while I do not like war, and cannot by any stretch of the imagination be said to wish that we ever have another one, unfortunately we have not yet any assurance that we shall have the permanent peace we all hope for but still are not too sure of.
We have our obligations to defend ourselves in the event of attack, which I hope never takes place. We have our obligation to the united nations organization when and if the security council makes some decision as to what Canada's part should be, and we must be ready to play that part if we believe what we say when we are members of the united nations. I am not particularly impressed by the minister's statement that we need military forces here for peace, order and good government in Canada. It has been a long time since the citizens of Canada have required anything more than a little bit of caution from the regular police forces to keep us in order. Generally we do not do much that requires a regiment of soldiers to come and prevent us from doing what we might be supposed to be doing.
I want to point out to the committee that there does not seem to be the urgency in this matter that some seem to indicate in their speeches. I would remind the committee that yesterday the Ottawa Journal, evening edition, carried what they said was a report of a statement made by Mr. L. B. Pearson at the secret session of the external affairs committee to which members of parliament and members of the other place were invited. I would never mention this myself, but I took it from the Journal, so that somebody must have told them and they reported that Mr. Pearson predicted that, in his opinion, there was no danger of a war before 1959. And we are led to believe that Mr. Pearson's opinion is something to which it is worth while giving consideration.
That being the case, considering the type of establishment the minister has envisaged in his statements, in answer to questions, it seems to me that he has time enough to introduce a well-coordinated scheme for national defence and training. This afternoon and at other times i't has been pointed out that the Canadian army did an excellent job in both world war I and world war II, and without a great deal of previous training. That is true. There are others who point out that a considerable time was needed between the day

we entered the war and the time we had the troops trained, and we could not afford to be unprepared the next time.
I agree with that, but I do not agree with the ideas put forward for preparedness. I want to remind the committee that before world war II, and in the early part of the war, there were many people in this country and in Europe who thought the Mannerheim line and the Maginot lines were good forms of preparedness. But when they came to be attacked by a modern force they were entirely out of date and therefore the preparedness they represented was not preparedness at all. I have no doubt the Maginot line, as a line of fortifications, wa!s well built and well equipped, if it represented all that the builders expected it to be, but it did not meet the needs of the blitzkrieg or the lightning warfare that came upon it at that time. It is equally possible that anything we may envisage now in the way of physical facilities would not be adequate if war came in 1959 or thereabouts. The kind of fitness and preparedness that is always in order is the physical and mental and moral fitness of our citizens. That is the most important fitness and preparedness that Canada can visualize. I believe the lack of that fitness was an important factor in our unpreparedness in the opening days of world war II. Time and again it has been stated that forty-seven per cent of those who submitted themselves for enlistment in our forces were physically unfit. Had those forty-seven per cent all been fit, as they should have been, and as a national plan before that would have made them, they would have been ready for their military duties much sooner and in greater numbers than they were. The same condition might have applied in our war and other industries if the same physical examination had taken place. The same weaknesses and unfitness might have been disclosed there. If they were there-and I believe they were-.then undoubtedly Canadian productive industry, including agriculture, mining and all others, suffered to the extent that probably forty-seven per cent of the workers were in the same physical category as those who offered themselves for the armed services. If we are to have a well-coordinated and well-planned defence equipment in this country we must have it powered by men and women who are themselves physically fit. Everything that goes to make that military establishment an efficient machine for Canada's defence and every one of the other industries must be powered by men and women who are physically fit and able to attain all the skills and speeds necessary to do the job at that time.

This afternoon the hon. member for Regina City mentioned the fact that there is a tendency sometimes for our military authorities to decide, for reasons of their own, that it is necessary to move a body of troops from one place to another. I know there was a terrific movement in war time. I remember one sailor telling me that he had joined the navy at Esquimalt, had immediately been posted to Halifax away from his home in Esquimalt, and had served out of Halifax and saved up his leave, which I believe could be done then, so that he might have enough leave to spend a nice Christmas at Esquimalt. A couple of years after he finally achieved that leave which he had saved up for, and went across the continent on that leave thinking he was going to have a happy Christmas with his family. He just landed at Esquimalt when he received a wire from Halifax to report back to duty. He galloped back across the country and reported for duty; he marched in, saluted' and said, "Here I am, sir, in accordance with the instructions in the telegram." He was immediately told that he had been reposted to a ship in Esquimalt; so back he went there again. I do not know whether that happened very often, but that was the story I heard.
It was good for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

If it is necessary in peace time, while troops are being trained and while we are building up this country for peace and for war, if war does come, instead of moving troops from one place to another by train, let the department organize and assemble all the necessary troops, working, engineering and others. If we are to take troops from a point "A" to a point "B" in Canada, let them build a road as they go along; then, when they get to "B" the road will be built, and from then on they will be able to get back and forth on it without using the railroads. And goodness knows, if we never again have a war, we still need plenty of roads. One could mention similar things all the way through, but I offer those suggestions for the minister's consideration in the hope that he will integrate some ideas like that in his new defence plan.
I want to ask the minister a question on his statement, in particular on point No. 10. As it appears in the paper-as I said before, I believe it is correct-it reads in this way:
Support for Canadian Arsenals Limited and a limited number of Canadian industries to maintain and increase skills in the design and manufacture of munitions and aircraft.
I am not questioning the minister's integrity in this. I am asking him why it says a limited number of Canadian industries? Would not all Canadian industries, in some form or another, be required in any kind of defence plan? I should like the minister to explain that to me. Then point No. 14 reads as follows:
Cooperation with the countries of the commonwealth-
With which I heartily agree.

the United States and other like-minded countries in working out common standards, planning and training.
The phrase "like-minded countries" is a rather loose one. They are like us in some respects; we are like them in some respects; but we also differ in some respects. I should like us to be like-minded in many more things before we start to standardize our military equipment. I should like us to be so like-minded that we standardize our agricultural equipment, as a result of which every tractor combine, mowing machine or cream separator made here or in the United States, may have a screw or bolt bought for it which will fit in any place. That would be what I would call like-mindedness. I should also like them to let our wheat in there without the 42-cent tariff. I should like us to let their radios in here without any tariff on them. I should like many of those things to come about before we can say that we are like-minded to them or that they are like-minded to us. I do not think we should just plan for our defence equipment.
I know that, in the opinion of others, it might interfere with some of the profit industries of this country. But again I draw to the attention of the committee that if we, unfortunately, some day have to go to war again, then profit and- all other privileges of citizens will have to take not only second place, but a place quite low down on the list in comparison with other national needs. Therefore, when we start to standardize, let us try to get others to be so friendly toward us and let us try to be so friendly toward them that we can forget some of our little past traditions of protected profitmaking enterprise and have complete free trade and free exchange right across the border.
In conclusion, I wish to ask the minister a question which he was asked this afternoon but did not reply to. The hon. member for Regina City asked the minister this question about military properties which have been turned over to War Assets: To what extent have properties been turned over to War Assets Corporation and then others bought to replace those disposed of? There is a good deal of
Supply-National Defence

feeling in parts of the country that too much of that sort of thing has gone on, that some individuals have reaped the benefit, and that the Canadian taxpayers must now replace those things which went for little, or certainly not enough, to private individuals and which must be replaced as military equipment.

I shall reply at once to the hon. member for Swift Current with regard to his last question. Referring to the question asked by the hon. member for Regina City as to what properties had been turned over to War Assets Corporation and then other properties bought in order to replace them, I can answer, absolutely none by the Department of National Defence, and I do not know of any by any other government department.
The other question the hon. member asked, to which I think I should refer, was in relation to point No. 10 in the objectives I set out, which reads:
Support for Canadian Arsenals Limited and a limited number of Canadian industries to maintain and increase skills in the design and manufacture of munitions and aircraft.
If I had not put in the word "limited" I am sure someone would have asked, how much support; for what industries; how can we support all industries; why should we support industries, and so on? The fact is there are a limited number of Canadian industries which have developed special skills in the production of munitions and aircraft which are not economic in peace time but which it is valuable to continue and which can be continued with a certain limited amount of assistance through orders, and the like; and we hope to be able to assist a very limited number of industries in the way I have indicated.

Without being too critical, I think the minister might well have worded the paragraph a little more clearly. If he had said, "those industries which are especially equipped" in the way he has just described, we would have understood.
I should think that would be understood by anyone.

I have no desire to make a speech, but I want to ask a question. In referring to that branch of the service which won both wars, my understanding of the answer given by the minister to the previous speaker was that a private in the army will receive the same pay as the corresponding rank in the air force. Is that correct?
Right.

Then I want to ask the minister this question so that his answer will be on record. What pay does a private

in the army receive? I do not know whether you have two ranks for privates in the army now, but I also want to know what pay is received by an L.A.C., which I believe is the correct term for the man in the air force. I have a couple more questions, the answers to which I want on record also. They slipped it over on the army during the war, and they are not going to do so in peace time if I have anything to say about the matter. I am an army man. I want to know what uniform the private or corresponding rank in the air force gets; what uniform and equipment the private in the army gets, and whether they get the same treatment in the army in regard to transportation as they get in the air force. In order to explain to the minister what I mean, during the war when a private was being taken across Canada he went in a colonist car, while an L.A.C. in the air force went in a tourist car. I have every respect for the air force, but no one can tell me that an air force man needs sheets more than an army man. I can tell the minister I am serious about this. I want to know definitely, and I want it on the record, what is the pay of every rank in the army and every rank in the air force? I am speaking of other ranks now, because when you get up to the generals and vice-admirals they are all air marshals or something like that, particularly when they want to be superannuated and get a pension. Is there any difference in any shape or form between the treatment given a private in the army and that given an L.A.C. in the air force? If so, what is the difference, and why?

The pay of all equivalent ranks in the three services was put on exactly the same basis and at the same rates last year. The basic rate of pay for a private on entry is S50; for a trained private, $54; for a private first class, $61; after three years, $64, and after six years, $67. In addition there is a separation allowance and a marriage allowance, which are exactly the same for the three services. All other conditions of service I can think of, including pensions, are identical for the three services. The uniforms still have some differences-
Oh, yes.

They are different
uniforms.
And the air force gets the best.

The navy, the army and the air force do wear different uniforms; but there is a committee of the three services called the senior supply officers committee, and another one called the personnel members committee, of the top people of the three

Supply-National Defence
services in those two fields, which have to clear all mew provisions, and any existing differences are being worked! out. I must say' I share the view of the hon. member who has just spoken. I could see no reason why three Canadians who enlisted from the same house and Who happened to wear the uniforms of the navy, the army and the air force, should have received duripg the war different rates of pay, different scales of rations and different uniforms. Except for the uniforms that are essential to the functioning of their services and in accordance with their traditions, our aim-and we are rapidly approaching it-is to have them on exactly the same basis for all three services. I believe that all three services are on exactly the same basis in every other particular.
Then will the minister answer my question as to the rates of pay? I understand that he has given them for the army?
Yes.
Now will he give me the rates of pay for members of the air force, so that- there will be no misunderstanding?

The ranks in the air
force are aircraftman second class, equivalent to a private on entry; aircraftman first class, equivalent to a private, trained; leading aircraftman, equivalent to private first class. Exactly the same rates of pay prevail for the same service.
In other words, there is no difference between a private in the army and a private in the air force, whatever he is called?
An aircraftman; no.

Then suppose you are moving an army man from Camp Borden to the best camp you have in Canada, at Chilliwack, and you are also moving a man the same day from Camp Borden, where you have some air force men, in Patricia Bay; do they have the same accommodation on the trains, whether they are on leave or on duty; if so, when did that come into effect?
For every equivalent rank in the three services the transportation allowance, living allowance and subsistence allowance while travelling are identical.

I have been waiting so long to make a few remarks on this matter that if I had not a fairly good memory I would have completely forgotten what I was going to talk about. I am sorry I was not in the house this morning for the major portion
of the minister's statement. However, from the report in the newspapers and the comment I have heard, together with the way in which he has answered the questions which have been asked this afternoon and this evening, I believe I must express my appreciation and, I am sure, the appreciation of a large number of other people for the marked increase over the past two years in the frankness and, I think I can say, the definiteness he has shown in giving parliament the general policy in regard to defence, and in answering questions. Perhaps this improvement may be due to the fact that the minister is an ex-gunner, as are a considerable number of members of the house, including myself, I am glad to say; and that as a result he learned to shoot straight and has not forgotten. However that may be, I hope it will not be taken as any reflection on any other service. I should like the hon. member for Fraser Valley particularly to remember that some two years ago I made a plea to make the pay of infantrymen in action the highest of any servicemen. I still believe that would be a reasonable move.
However I wish to speak chiefly about the reserve army. I believe the minister knows that for many years before the war I had and at the present time still have an interest in the reserve army. Between the last session of parliament and this one, I believe I saw and talked to, at various conferences, nearly every commanding officer of reserve units in Alberta. Among them I found a general feeling such as that expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard; it is a feeling of discouragement. In some instances the commanders of these reserve force units were ready to give up, and in each instance the cause of discouragement was that they found it extremely difficult to stir up interest among the younger men in their respective communities to get them to enlist in reserve force units.
They were almost universal in their belief that this lack of interest was due to the fact that the government had not stated a definite defence policy. However I believe the minister's statement of this afternoon will go some distance toward correcting that condition. They were further convinced of the fact that when such a statement of policy was made- and they believed it should be made immediately-it should be publicized and that the department should take means to bring home to the general citizens of Canada the fact that the reserve army is necessary, and that it is the duty of ablejbodied young men to devote a certain amount of their time to reserve army, air force or naval training, as the case may be.

I believe these men, whose experience covered the province, were correct. I do not believe we shall have a successful reserve army, nor shall we be able to recruit our reserve force units up to any reasonable strength until steps are taken to impress upon the general public the fact that the defence army is necessary and that every encouragement should be given to people to join reserve units.
I was glad to hear the minister mention citizens' committees this afternoon which, I believe, were set up in every locality in Alberta to increase interest and to give support to the reserve units in their particular communities. I believe, however, the minister was under some slight misapprehension as to who started those committees. The man responsible for that was Colonel Eric Snow, who at that time was in command of military district No. 13. My information is that he evolved the idea and had some of the committees started. The idea seemed such a good one that General Worthington then introduced it into his whole command. I believe that since that time an effort has been made to make it effective throughout Canada. I would ask the minister to indicate what success the movement has had and to what extent citizens' committees have been established throughout Canada, because I believe they will prove, with proper support by way of publicity from the government, one of the most potent means of making our reserve army a success.
I believe the whole question of our reserve army policy should be given more thought. I am very doubtful, as are other reserve force officers, as to the possibilities of a six-division reserve force. The minister said this afternoon it was never intended that all the units of these six reserve force divisions would be brought up to full strength. However, so far I have been able to observe, an effort has been made to activate all or practically all those of any size. The result is that in a city like Calgary with a population of about
100,000	we have three regiments of artillery. It is true that the batteries of two of those regiments are scattered. Then, we have an infantry battalion, a tank regiment, a complete divisional army service corps set-up, or at least a lieutenant-colonel's command of army service corps. We have an engineers company, a field ambulance corps, an ordnance corps, a signals company and so on.
To bring those units up to strength would require, I should think, at least 7,000 men. There just are not 7,000 young men in Calgary, and there are not going to be-indeed I do not think there should be the hope that there

would be-who will be willing to serve in the *reserve army under anything like present circumstances. In addition, the navy and the air force are bidding for the services of these young men.
1 Considerable thought should be given to the whole scheme of a six-division reserve army. I do not believe Canada can possibly support it, and I do not believe we can get the men into it. We were not able to support six divisions during the last war, and had trouble to support five. It seems to me that the scheme is too ambitious, and should be recast to something which would be more capable of efficient operation. I offer that suggestion to the minister in the hope that it will be 'received in the spirit in which it has been offered, namely, one of sincere desire for the improvement and success of the reserve army.
There is one other observation by the minister with respect to the reserve army upon which I should like to comment. He said that in the past year an effort has been made to secure a training nucleus of officers, noncommissioned officers and staffs, with administrative and training officers in each unit. Theoretically that sounds all right; but from the practical point of view and from experience, let me .tell the minister that if a group of officers and non-commissioned officers have no men to train they lose interest, because they have nothing to do. It is practically hopeless to attempt to bring down a group of officers and non-commissioned officers once or twice a week to have them go through a course of training when they have no men to train and to work with. In other words, in actual practice and from experience I know this just does not work out, although theoretically it may appear all right. If the minister expects the reserve army to be a success efforts must be made to get men into the reserve units. In fact, they must be got in, or the nucleus of officers and non-commissioned officers will disappear, so that we shall have nothing.
Somebody told me that the minister had said that there would be some sort of recruiting scheme carried on this fall. Will that be for the permanent force or for the reserve force as well?
Both.

I am glad to hear that. I should like the minister to tell the committee on what scale it is to be carried on and what form it will take. I do not want him to go into details, but perhaps he can give us a general idea of what is to be done along that line. It certainly is mcessary. The

minister was to give some figures to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard in regard to the numbers in a typical reserve army unit. When he is giving those figures, will he give the number of men in the reserve army by commands?
The reason I ask that- is this. The people in Alberta are extremely interested in knowing what is the situation. Some six to eight months ago, when most of the commanding officers were discouraged over the situation, army officials were telling them that the situation in the reserve units in the west, particularly in Alberta, was the best in the dominion, that they were doing very well and to keep up the good work. They were told that they had more men than anywhere else in the dominion. The general idea among those men at that time was that if that was the case the reserve force was certainly in a bad way. Therefore I should like the minister to put those figures on the record.
There are one or two other points in connection with the permanent force brigade group matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver South. There is no doubt that in 1945 and 1946 we were assured that this brigade group would be an absolutely up-to-scratch force which would be trained for airborne operations and would be ready to move more or less on one or two days notice against any small attack which might be made. In other words, it was to be an up-to-the-minute force capable of immediate activity. We are now told that it has a strength of only some 2,000 men, that it is scattered all over the country and that there is no idea of bringing it together as a group. It seems to me that you have not a brigade group at all; you have not anything. All you have are men scattered here and there over the country who are not serving any useful purpose as a fighting force. They may be serving a useful purpose for training certain reserve units, for providing a training ground for permanent force officers and so on, but that is about all.
There is a disproportionate number of people, it seems to me, employed at national defence headquarters, on command staffs and so on. That number should be cut down a bit and this brigade group built up into a force of which we would be proud, into a fighting force. During the war it was found beneficial to switch men from staff duties to regimental duties. That policy was generally followed, and I would suggest to the minister that men be switched from the brigade group to staff jobs of various sorts and from staff jobs to 83166-341
the brigade group. I think that would be most beneficial as far as our permanent force is concerned.

The hon. member must know that- those kinds of changes go on steadily. For example, the commanding officer of one of the active force units at Calgary was recently moved to take a staff course. On the other point, there is no intention not to activate and form into one outfit this brigade group.
I did not think there were enough in the brigade group to permit changes.

It is coming along. With regard to the number of units, I carry the figure in my head. In order to constitute a six-division army out of 180,000 men of the reserve in Canada it would take about 2,000 units. At the present time we have somewhere in the neighbourhood of 650 units. My hon. friend will see that his idea is already being acted upon.
Mr. Harkness:	It is mainly the larger
units which have been activated, rather than the small units?

In a country like Canada it is most important to have units where the population is. For example, a'unit like the South Saskatchewan, which probably was not very active in peace time, was one of the best regiments we had in war-time. The fact that it had a nucleus in existence enabled it to mobilize and raise its officers and noncommissioned officers rapidly, so that it proved a useful thing to have.
The hon. member asked what success had attended the effort to have citizens' committees throughout the country. That is not a new thing. For years units have had Committees back of them. What is new is that, possibly at Colonel Sims' suggestion, General Worthington made it universal throughout his whole command. As the hon. member said, that has been a great success, and I think it is spreading throughout other commands.
To what extent has it been successful throughout the others?

It has spread gradually as units can form committees or as committees can be formed for units. It has not been applied as an order, because this is the kind of thing which should grow spontaneously in the community under the encouragement of the G.O.C. of the command or the officers commanding the unit. It is being encouraged and worked on.

With the other remarks of the hon. meniber I have a great deal of sympathy, and I will give consideration to a great deal of what he has said. With regard to the general policy in connection with the reserve, the policy has been to form, first, a nucleus of officers and non-commissioned officers. That is following largely along the lines of the discussions we had with the reserve representatives. I can remember several of them saying that they had to get going on the basis of officers and non-commissioned officers and tradesmen strength before they could do very much with men. As the hon. member and all those familiar with this will agree, it is a question of timing. As soon as you get the officer and non-commissioned officer and unit organization working, then you must get the men for them to train. We are trying to work on that timing as well as we can.

Before saying a word on the Royal Canadian Sea Cadets, I should like to say that I was pleased to hear the minister state this morning that living quarters would soon be available for married personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy in the Halifax area. I know he knows that there are many cases where great hardship has been experienced. I have had several cases brought to my attention where families have had to live hundreds of miles from Halifax. I know of one case where the family needed fatherly discipline. The man was interested in his work in the navy but, because his family had to live hundreds of miles away, he became greatly dissatisfied with his situation. As I say, I was pleased to bear the minister state that that situation would soon be rectified.
We are going to do our utmost to correct it as soon as we can.

In connection with the Royal Canadian Sea Cadets, as I said before in this house, I know of no movement in Canada over the past few years which has done so much for the youth of this country. It is not a flash in the pan. The Navy League of Canada has been operating for years. A great deal of the personnel of our Canadian navy of the past years was furnished and made available because of the Royal Canadian Sea Cadets movement. In that connection I should like to quote Frank S. Rutherford, deputy minister of education of Ontario. He was appointed a few months ago. He said in part:
My association with the navy league sea cadet movement has convinced me that the training provided is essentially good, whether a young man enters the navy or civilian employment. Naval training presents opportunities for the use of mind and hand which are bound to be affected in any type of employment.

The associations which a young man will make in the sea cadets will be lasting and most helpful in the years to come.
I would go a step farther than that, and I believe the minister will agree with me. The Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps have within their ranks reserves for the navy of tomorrow or when they are desired. I would urge the minister to give every consideration to expanding that service. I know that a few months ago the cadet services were curtailed, and through negotiations with the navy league, I believe, certain adjustments were made. But there is one point I should like to draw to the minister's attention, which is one I brought up in the house some few months ago.
About a year ago, the sea cadet training officers were put on pay by the Department of National Defence. At that time I suggested that the remuneration should be in the form of clothing allowances and not as pay, because when it is given in the form of pay it is added to their income and the greater part of it is wiped out in income tax; it does not meet the purpose for which it was intended. Over the years, the sea cadets have given of their time and of their money. I know that, because I have been more or less actively engaged in the movement. They are constantly using their cars and different things to further the movement. When they are given pay it certainly does not go anywhere near recompensing them for the time and energy they put in the movement.
I should like to mention one other point. Certain curtailments were made in the size of corps, and there was also a restriction put on the units going to camp this year. Originally they were to go for one week. That was changed by the defence department and they were allowed the two weeks training as they had previously enjoyed, but the size of the unit that was allowed to go to camp was practically cut in half. One corps in which I am directly interested of one hundred cadets and officers was allowed to send to camp this year only forty cadets and two officers. I wish to bring that to the minister's attention, because it is discouraging to these boys, and especially to some of the boys who have worked hard all year in the hope that they would be selected to go to camp. It is a hardship; it is a discouragement to the officers and boys who are training. It should be considered and a change should be made, if not this year, next year to remedy the situation.
In closing, I wish to say that the sea cadet movement of Canada is one of the finest youth training schemes we have had. In its ranks you have the reserve navy of tomorrow.

I wish to ask the minister a few questions with regard to cadet training in Canada, but before I do so I want to say a few words about the statement which he gave this morning .which, as has already been said, is perhaps the first clear statement we have had since this parliament convened as to what would be our defence policy. Some of the things which were pointed out a short time ago by the hon. member for Swift Current as to bringing the training of our forces into a form which will make certain that they are attractive to all people of the country so that it will be realized there is a real career in the service for men of ability and activity, are important. They have been said before in the house. I shall not go over them, but I should like to emphasize what seems to me to be one of the most essential things today, and I hope that that aspect of the matter will be emphasized in the recruiting programme which the -minister has indicated will be brought into effect this fall; giving our engineers practical work to do in the country which will make a contribution, not only to their training, but to the development of the country; giving the signal corps in the various services practical work in the construction of communication systems, which will not only be of value to them as training but be of value in building up the communication system of Canada. These things should be emphasized so that the training of our forces will equip them, in order that when they retire from the forces at the reduced age which is now in effect they will be able to take their place in the civilian life of the country on an equal footing with other persons who have not been in the forces, but who have perhaps been on a superior level because their training and experience will all have been practical.
With regard to the cadet programme for Canada, I should like to say at the outset, as has just been said by the hon. member for Wentworth with reference to the navy, the cadet corps in this country are certainly the pool from which normally one would expect the armed services to be drawn.
At the outset one should pay a tribute to the work which has been done by civilian personnel and by officers in connection with cadet training. It would not be proper to stop at that. One should also pay a tribute to the provinces in this field, and to the work of the ministries of education of rthe various provinces. We recall that during the war they were urged to try to bring up their cadet training programme so that practically one hundred per cent of -those attending secondary 83166-341J
schools would be receiving cade't training. It is a fact perhaps worth recording that in some of the provinces, in one at any rate, a programme was worked out by agreement with the Department of National Defence, so that one hundred per cent of those boys in secondary schools would receive cadet training. The importance of this is not only in the military value which those younig men themselves will get from it, and therefore our armed forces will get, but the value to the whole country in training in citizenship which will follow and the contribution to the health and welfare of our youth. Perhaps these aspects are as important as the military value which can be derived from any cnde-t scheme.
In the light of these remarks I should like to refer briefly to an outline of the programme given by the -minister on February 17, at whic-h time he indicated to the house that, although certain reductions were contemplated, it was not intended actually to reduce the number of cadet corps in training in this country. The minister said that, following the end of the present school year, army cadet training would be organized in two types, open corps affiliated with reserve corps units and school corps sponsored by boards of education, some of which are also affiliated with reserve units. At the end of that statement on February 17 he said, as reported at page 506 of Hansard:
There will be no reduction in the number of cadet corps of boys who fall within the classes I mentioned, aged fourteen to eighteen, provided that they are organized in corps of twenty or more.
Sin-ce that time there have been indications that there is a substantial reduction in the number of cadets authorized to receive training in our schools throughout the country. I suppose that might have been done partly as an economy measure. Certainly it was indicated that some saving was to be effected by it. We all realize that saving is essential; but it seems to me, since the major contribution to cadet training is made by the provinces in the schools in which the training is taken, the saving will be negligible. I think I could go so far as to say it is another typical case where the government is taking a step in the wrong direction and at the wrong time, because the value of this cadet training, in terms of citizenship and in increase in health and welfare in the country, cannot be measured in terms of the money expended on it. The saving itself is certainly negligible and far more than offset by the value that would be derived from a thoroughgoing scheme of cadet training.

I would ask the minister some questions with regard to the present programme. Were notices sent out by the Department of National Defence or the various headquarters or any of them in the country to school principals that they must reduce the number of cadets in training?

Yes, certainly. The cadets in respect of whom the federal government would pay the grants would be cadets in schools who had entered in September, in the 9th grade, and were under eighteen years of age, and in open corps cadets between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. That was gone into fully in the house on February 17 when the same question was asked and the same answer given. As far as I know, it has been acted on.
In the light of that statement I would ask whether any notice was given at that time to the provincial governments and the ministers of education concerned that this cut would be made.

The question of defence is a federal matter. The designation of the cadets in respect of whom the federal government pays money voted by parliament for defence purposes is a federal matter. It always has been and I do not know why it should not be. The question of cadets regarding whom federal grants are paid has always been a matter for federal determination. The communication was issued, as far as I know, in exactly the same way as all other communications have been issued with regard to cadets.

The point is that there was in effect in one province an agreement made with the Department of National Defence and approved by the then ministers of national defence, that they would train all their boys in secondary schools, and they were prepared to pay their share of the cost of doing that. It seems that, subsequent to that agreement, notices were sent out from various defence establishments in the country that they would be required to cut down the number of cadets in training. I would ask whether any arrangement was sought to be reached with the provincial governments in that connection, since the provincial governments made their contribution and their ministers of education were anxious to continue cadet training. It is unfortunate the attitude was taken that this is so exclusively a federal matter, that we had already reached an agreement with the provinces, that there should be unilateral action to vary that agreement without consultation with provinces which were anxious to continue such training.

Notification was made in this case, as in all other cases where there have been changes. Agreements were made with all the provinces in 1911 under the Strathcona trust and during the thirty years since, the Department of National Defence, under various names, has made changes in accordance with the votes and provisions for training, and those changes have been notified as they have been made. I have never heard it suggested* before that, prior to making any change, the Department of National Defence should secure the acquiescence or agreement of each of the nine provinces. That is a new notion.

Perhaps not with each of the nine before the department makes anjr change in any one province; but certainly, inasmuch as cadets are trained in the secondary schools, if there is to be a change in the basis on which training is given, I should imagine the intention to make the change and the working out of the change would be a matter of consultation with tlhe province.
There are in every command cadet officers available for consultation, and they consult with the local educational officers.

I recall that sometime earlier this year a public statement was made by the premier of one province to the effect that in that province they were willing and anxious to continue, and I believe he went so far as to say they would continue, cadet training in their secondary schools for all boys in those schools. I want to know whether the minister has received any official communications from any provincial minister of education asking that he reconsider the position and inquiring whether the department will not enter into consultation with the provinces to work out some scheme whereby universal cadet training in secondary schools can be continued.

The only communication received from any provincial educational authority was one I received last week from the minister of education of Ontario. The communication was dated June 25. It was the first I had heard from a provincial minister with regard to this matter and I made a reply. The officers of the department of education concerned with cadets and the officers of the Department of National Defence were in communication back at the end of February and the beginning of March, but these direct communications were stopped, and this is the first I have heard about it since.

The direct communications were stopped? That, I think, is unfortunate.
