I think it is very unfortunate. They were stopped by the province of Ontario.
Well, the public statement made by the minister of education of Ontario was to the effect that they desired to continue 100 per cent cadet training in their schools.
We shall be glad to cooperate with them on the terms we announced.
What was the last communication received-June 25? Was that a request to reopen negotiations?

I do not suppose I should table that letter without the consent of the premier. I certainly have no objection to tabling it, or yet my reply, but that letter was one in which he referred to a state of uncertainty in the province of Ontario with regard to this matter and to his own attitude. Until I secure some consent from him to tabling the letter, I probably should not go any farther. The fact is that the first sign of any difficulty that came to my attention as a result of the communication from the province of Ontario was this letter of June 25, which was just about four months after the announcement of policy I had made; a little more than four months.
Is the minister considering a revision of the policy or some steps to enable-

No. We have announced that we are not in favour of continuing junior cadets, and we propose to make federal grants from the federal treasury with respect to senior cadets; that is, cadets generally speaking in school cadet corps who enter the ninth grade on September 1, and who have not reached the age of eighteen, and in open corps who, are between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. We do not propose any more to make grants in respect of junior cadets. That is a definite government and department policy arrived at, we think, for sound reasons, and we have no disposition whatever to change that. I do not think there is any desire on the part of the country that we should.
Have the department any objections, or have they made any representations against the provinces continuing cadet training outside of the categories which the minister has just mentioned?

I have not had any representations with regard to cadets from any province except Ontario, and the letter of the
minister of education does not suggest extending the ages. He does not deal with the question of ages.

I hope my hon. friend
opposite is through with his questions. I have only two questions to ask the minister, andi they are clearcut, concise and precise. I hope the minister will be kind enough to give me a clear answer. In the first place, I want to know if the experts of his department believe that Canada will be the theatre of the next war. In the second place, I want to know if we can expect peace-time compulsory training this year, or if it has been put aside for some time.
Before the minister answers, I will draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that the discussion has been going on for a whole day on item 551. There is another item, 552, in the demobilization and reconversion part of the estimates. Then at page 25 of the estimates there are ten other items which are as yet untouched. As I look at the list, I see that we still have quite a large number of items to pass. There is the auditor general, finance, part of fisheries, governor general and lieutenant governors, insurance, labour, legislation, mines and resources; all of national defence, all of labour, all of mines and resources, all of national revenue-

Yes; and the Prime Minister's office, privy council office, reconstruction and supply, veterans affairs, loans and investments; and under demobilization and reconversion, auditor general, finance, fisheries, labour, mines and resources, national defence, privy council office, reconstruction and supply, trade and commerce and veterans affairs. There are several hundred items. If we do not catch a fast train, we shall stay here for a long time, and we can say good-bye to summer as we did last year. This is not a lecture to anyone; it is an olive branch that I show to all.
The hon. member had better sit down.

As I say, it is an olive branch that I show to all, in the expectation that there will be a certain spirit of cooperation and that we shall all do our best to bring the session to an end. I may tell you, Mr. Chairman, that I had some very fine stuff about the brass hats, about the dealings of the Canadian Department of National Defence, the British government, the United States government, the United States army, the British army and so on; but I have put all that

aside, to think it over, and have not said a word about it. I asked two short questions about matters of general concern. I hope there will be more of a spirit of conciliation. Members may ask questions, as we have heard them ask them all day, but it will not change a single vote in the great old city of Halifax on Monday next. This must be kept in mind.
